findings.claim: Epidemic Sound's Partner API is not self-serve for production: a partnership agreement is required, and the free developer plan is prototyping-only with no commercial licence.
findings.evidence: Docs: 'To use the Epidemic Sound API, you need a partnership agreement. Once your agreement is in place, your technical team members will be added to the Developer Portal and receive credentials to start building.' 'The Free plan is for prototyping. It includes the full catalogue of music and sound effects and every endpoint except safelisting, with up to 50 downloads and no commercial licence, so you can't go live on it.' 'The API Developer License covers evaluating, prototyping and testing your app on the Free plan, and it doesn't cover production or commercial use.' 'Scale is priced on download volume, and Enterprise has a contract tailored to your use case.'

findings.claim: Under the Epidemic Partner API, the end user's rights depend on the end user's own Epidemic subscription linked via 'ES Connect'; free-tier users only get a personal licence.
findings.evidence: FAQ: 'Users with an active paid Epidemic Sound subscription connected to your app through ES Connect receive a commercial user license' (covering monetization and advertising use); free-tier music 'gives users a personal license for posting online'. Developer page: 'a simple safelisting system lets platforms like YouTube, Instagram, TikTok, Facebook, Twitch, and more know that the music is licensed correctly.' Catalogue scope is 'negotiated as part of your partnership agreement (curated collections or full catalogue)'.

findings.claim: Epidemic Sound's Commercial subscription licence (the tier a barber business would need) covers publishing productions anywhere online including social platforms, allows sub-licensing, but excludes offline broadcast/TV, covers one user, and caps the business's turnover.
findings.evidence: Licence text: you may 'publish your Productions anywhere online, meaning on websites, on social media platforms and video sharing platforms, in apps, and anywhere else online'; 'You may sub-license or transfer the rights to make available such Productions to any third party.'; limits include no offline broadcast or TV use, no theme songs or trademarks; the company 'must not have an annual turnover of more than USD fifty (50) million'; 'The license covers only one user.' Personal single-track licence by contrast is 'intended solely for your own personal use' and 'you may only monetize the Production on one (1) single YouTube channel'. Business plan: 'cleared for business use across marketing, social, internal communications, and client work', for 'brands with under $10M annual revenue'. Single-track Commercial licence '$99.99 per track'. Billing: 'You can cancel whenever you want and still use the music, sound effects, and tools until your next renewal period.'

findings.claim: Soundstripe is the most accessible 'real' music API for a small developer: a self-serve 30-day trial key exists, but production keys (and the licence that covers end users) require a sales/enterprise agreement.
findings.evidence: Enterprise API page: 'Hit "Create key" to generate your trial API key, valid for 30 days'; 'Trial keys are watermarked and expire after 30 days. High-res files need a production key.' Docs: 'Content must be served to users via Soundstripe's CDN'; 'Client-side communication with the servers is strictly prohibited, since API keys are privileged'; standard rate limit '25 requests per second per API key'. Pricing FAQ: Enterprise 'includes API access and up to $1 million in indemnity', custom priced. API Terms: 'any use of the Soundstripe Library, through Soundstripe's API or otherwise, shall be in accordance with the license(s) granted to you and restrictions contained in the Terms of Use.'

findings.claim: Soundstripe plan coverage: Personal excludes paid social; Pro covers commercial content incl. digital ads for individuals; Business covers brand-owned content with paid social for a local audience; downloads used while subscribed stay licensed after cancellation.
findings.evidence: Help-center pricing: 'Personal at $19.99/mo or $119/yr, Pro at $39.99/mo or $239/yr, Pro Plus at $69.99/mo or $399/yr, and Business at $299/quarter or $999/yr', Enterprise custom. 'Pro covers commercial content created by individuals, including client projects and digital ads and campaigns.' Business is 'designed for companies, agencies, or teams creating brand-owned or client-owned content within a single geographic market' with paid social 'limited to a local audience'; Personal column says 'Not included' for paid social. 'content you download and use in projects while subscribed stays licensed forever, though you can no longer use the content in new projects after you cancel.'

findings.claim: Artlist exposes a Music API only on its custom-priced Enterprise plan; the standard licence cannot be sublicensed or embedded in an app.
findings.evidence: Help centre: Enterprise includes 'direct integration, including the Artlist Music API' and 'a customizable license that allows for global distribution across client projects'; Enterprise covers 'use in apps, games, software, broadcasts, out-of-home (OOH) advertising, audiobooks, and more'. FAQ: the licence 'can not be transferred or sublicensed with our standard agreement'; 2021 licence PDF: 'if you want to add the Assets to your app or website you might need an Enterprise License'. Third-party profile (unconfirmed) describes Search API + Download API with OAuth 2.0 client-credentials.

findings.claim: Artlist's cheap Social plan is NOT valid for a business's promotional videos; business use needs Pro, Max Business or Enterprise.
findings.evidence: 'the Music and SFX Social plans come with a Social license, exclusively for personal content creators' covering 'a single channel on YouTube, TikTok, Facebook, Instagram, Twitch, and one podcast' and 'does not cover commercial or client work'. Licence page: the license 'does not allow you to create Projects that are intended to be uploaded or embedded on third party channels or websites for the purpose of promotion or advertisement'; 'on behalf of a company with more than 50 employees, an Enterprise plan or Max Business plan is required'. Pricing reported as Social Creator '$14.99 per month monthly or $9.99 per month annually' (launch blog) - conflicting figures elsewhere.

findings.claim: Uppbeat has no released API (it is 'in development'); free downloads are usable on Instagram/TikTok/YouTube only with an Uppbeat credit; paid Pro/Business plans remove attribution and cover commercial/business content.
findings.evidence: Uppbeat: 'currently developing an API which will allow you to access Uppbeat's library from within your own products and experiences'; pricing page invites sign-ups to 'be the first to get access to our new API'. Licence blog: 'All downloads (even on free plans!) are covered for use on social platforms like YouTube, TikTok and Instagram, as long as you include the required attribution – basically a quick credit to Uppbeat.' Pro: 'licensed for individuals, freelancers and solo professionals, covering your own content and client projects'; Business: 'teams, companies and organizations'. Pricing page: Pro '$14.99/month, billed yearly, or monthly for $24.99'; Business '$34.99/month excl. tax, billed yearly'. Broadcast/streaming/radio/cinema 'need a custom license'. Third-party: each free download generates a unique 'Uppbeat Credit' code that must be pasted into the description of one specific video.

findings.claim: Musicbed has no public API or developer program; its Personal plan excludes brand-affiliated work, so a barber business needs the Business plan.
findings.evidence: KB: the Personal plan 'does not cover client work, paid or unpaid, and is only for personal lifestyle or vlog content shared on personal channels. Brand-affiliated or product-selling work should use the Business or Enterprise plan.' Business plan 'covering client work for clients up to 250 employees'. Blog: subscription licences cover 'paid advertising, including social boosting, up to $5,000 in ad spend'. Reported pricing: '$29.99 per month' (no client work) and 'starting at $99.99 per month' for business/client work; single-song '$59.99' personal vs '$349.99' business. Searches restricted to musicbed.com found no API, developer or partner documentation.

findings.claim: Pixabay's public API covers images and videos only; there is no music/sound-effects endpoint. Pixabay music may be used in commercial videos without attribution, but some tracks are Content-ID registered.
findings.evidence: Official API page 'describes access to its images and videos'; apis.io lists only 'pixabay.com/api/' and 'pixabay.com/api/videos/'; 'music' appears only as an image category. FAQ: 'You may use Pixabay music in commercial video projects, including content you sell or distribute (such as client videos, promotional materials, or paid training content), as long as the music is part of a larger creative work and not distributed as a standalone file'; attribution 'isn't required'; some tracks 'registered with YouTube Content ID' (shield icon) and Pixabay advises 'keeping download records as proof of permitted use'.

findings.claim: Freesound's APIv2 is free only for non-commercial use; commercial API use needs a case-by-case licence from UPF, and each sound carries its own CC licence (CC0, CC BY, or CC BY-NC).
findings.evidence: API terms: 'Terms for commercial use of the API will be negotiated on a case by case basis with UPF, including limits regarding the volume of use of the Platform.' Rate limits: 60 requests/minute and 2,000/day; downloads/uploads etc. '30 requests per minute and 500 requests per day'; 'API throttling limits are applied at the "user" level, not at the "client" level.' FAQ lists CC0, CC BY and CC BY-NC; forum moderator: with CC-BY and CC-BY-NC 'you MUST attribute the author/authors', and ad revenue counts as commercial use.

findings.claim: Free Music Archive no longer offers an API, cannot itself license tracks, and its paid route is Tribe of Noise PRO per-track licences.
findings.evidence: 'FMA used to have an API that app developers could use to make FMA content available in their apps. Due to the heavy load this put on our servers we had to shut down the API.' License guide: 'FMA cannot license original work to you for commercial, private, or other use'; 'All songs are free, but not all of them can be used in videos, podcasts, short films or commercial projects.' Tribe of Noise PRO: 'with a small budget (€45 / ~US$50) you can search, find and license a song' with 'a Tribe of Noise PRO certificate'. Tribe of Noise acquired FMA on September 12, 2019.

findings.claim: ccMixter has a public (beta) Query API with a licence filter; only CC BY / CC0 results are safe for commercial promo videos and require credit; Sampling-licensed uploads cannot be used in advertising.
findings.evidence: Query API 2.0 (beta) 'lic' values include 'by', 'nc', 'sa', 'nod', combinations, Sampling and Public Domain; example 'limit=10&tags=sample&lic=by'. dig.ccMixter: the CC tier is 'free to use, even in commercial projects but you must give credit to the musicians'; forum: 'dig.ccmixter.org/free_music?dig-lic=safe does a proper search for "Free for commercial use"'. About page: 'uploads under the Sampling licenses can not be used in advertising or to promote anything other than the songs involved.' Attribution guide recommends track title, artist, link and licence link. 'Tunetrack' returned no results.

findings.claim: Incompetech (Kevin MacLeod) music is free under CC BY (3.0 on older tracks, 4.0 on newer) with mandatory credit, or a paid 'Standard License' removes attribution; no API.
findings.evidence: Licenses page: the CC tier is 'no charge, but it requires that you credit the music' and the site generates credit text; the paid Standard License is for 'projects where attribution is not wanted or is impossible' and grants 'worldwide distribution, not crediting me, and also not paying royalties' (fee shown blank on the sample contract). Third-party sources report US$30 for one song, $50 for two, $20 each for three or more, and a credit format of track title, 'Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com)', and the CC BY 4.0 licence link.

findings.claim: YouTube Audio Library has no API; official terms permit use in videos you create and monetize on YouTube, forbid standalone distribution, and require credit for CC tracks; use on other platforms is not explicitly addressed.
findings.evidence: Official channel text: 'music from this library is intended solely for use by you in videos and other content that you create'; 'you may use music files from this library in videos that you monetize on YouTube'; you 'may not make available, distribute or perform the music files from this library separately from videos'. Help: 'if you're using a track with a Creative Commons license, you must credit the artist in your video's description'; 'Attribution not required' filter = standard Audio Library licence. Separate Creator Music product: licences 'are not transferable to other platforms or other YouTube channels'. No YouTube Data API endpoint for the Audio Library appeared in any result.

findings.claim: TikTok's general sound library is personal/non-commercial only; a Business Account only sees Commercial Sounds, and Commercial Music Library tracks are licensed for use on TikTok only (not in MP4s posted elsewhere).
findings.evidence: Music Terms: general-library sounds are for 'personal, non-commercial use'; 'Any uses outside of the Platform require you to obtain separate permission and license the necessary rights directly from all necessary rights holders unless otherwise authorized by the Commercial Music Library - User Terms.' CML User Terms: 'Commercial Sounds can only be used within TikTok. Videos with these sounds may be posted or shared only on TikTok and through its sharing features'; 'Any platform not designated under the "Usable Placements" section should be considered not permitted unless the rights holder's consent is obtained'; off-platform uses such as 'posting videos on third party digital platforms' require 'separate permission and licensing the necessary rights directly from the Commercial Sound rights holder(s)'; 'Premium-designated tracks may require an additional fee.' Help centre: Business Account users who open Add Sound 'see only the CML's tracks, labeled Commercial Sounds'; 'Businesses cannot use the general music library for commercial usage.' Business Terms: for business purposes a creator can use the Commercial Sounds page or web CML 'or clear all music rights on their own'.

findings.claim: Any app posting to TikTok via the Content Posting API must display a Music Usage Confirmation consent line, and unaudited apps can only post privately.
findings.evidence: Content Sharing Guidelines: 'Before allowing users to post through your platform, there should be a declaration asking for a user's consent before the publish button'; standard wording 'By posting, you agree to TikTok's Music Usage Confirmation.' Music Usage Confirmation: the user confirms the video has no copyright-protected music or that they 'have obtained and paid for all necessary licenses' covering composition and master recording; 'If you cannot confirm (a) or (b) above then please do not accept.' Get Started: 'all content uploaded via this endpoint will be restricted to private viewing mode' for unaudited clients, 5 users per 24h, error 'unaudited_client_can_only_post_to_private_accounts'. Support: for content promoting a brand, product or service TikTok recommends the CML because tracks are pre-cleared.

findings.claim: Meta's Music Guidelines prohibit commercial/non-personal music use without licences and disclaim any authorisation; business use of Meta products also triggers the Commercial Terms.
findings.evidence: 'Use of music for commercial or non-personal purposes in particular is prohibited unless you have obtained appropriate licenses.' 'Keep in mind you remain solely responsible for the content that you post, including any music that is featured in that content. Nothing in these terms constitutes any authorization by us with respect to any use of music on any of our Products.' Guidance: 'If you want to utilize music not in the public domain or in Sound Collection, you should secure the appropriate licenses directly from the applicable rights holders for the applicable territories.' Terms of Service: business use means 'you must agree to our Commercial Terms' and 'If you post or share content containing music, you must comply with our Music Guidelines.' A 'music_guidelines_Jan2024' version exists.

findings.claim: Meta Sound Collection audio is licensed for commercial use but ONLY inside Meta products; it must not be baked into MP4s destined for TikTok, YouTube or a website.
findings.evidence: Sound Collection Terms: 'Meta hereby grants you a non-exclusive, royalty-free license to use the SC Audio Content for commercial or non-commercial purposes in content you create, upload, and distribute on the Meta Company Products, and you may not perform, distribute, make available or otherwise use the SC Audio Content separately from the Meta Company Products.' Meta 'can monitor or audit your compliance with these Terms and update these terms from time to time.' Library described as 'over 14,000 music tracks from established composers and songwriters and over 1,500 sound effects'.

findings.claim: Instagram business accounts may not have the Licensed Music Library; Meta's documented fallback is the Sound Collection or original audio, and boosted Reels/ads cannot use licensed music.
findings.evidence: Help: 'You're trying to access a song in our Licensed Music Library, but the library isn't available for your account type or in your country or region.' 'If you don't have access to the licensed music library, then you can add audio from our Sound Collection.' Boost help: use 'royalty-free music, like what's available in our Sound Collection, or original audio'. Ads help: Ads Manager music 'consists of royalty-free audio from the Meta Sound Collection' for Reels, Stories and Feed single-image ads. No official page listing which account types/countries get licensed music was captured; the Business Help page 'Access to the licensed music library on Instagram' exists but its wording was not retrievable.

findings.claim: 2026 change: Meta added an Instagram Audio API (June 1, 2026) that can attach Sound Collection/original audio to Reels at creation time via Facebook-Login apps, plus copyright detection fields for API-published media.
findings.evidence: Changelog: 'Introducing the Instagram Audio API for apps using Facebook Login. The API lets your app search for and retrieve audio — original sounds from Reels and royalty-free music from Meta's Sound Collection — and attach it to Reels at creation time.' Endpoints 'GET /ig_audio?audio_type={music|original_sound}' and 'GET /{ig_audio_id}'; also 'when a Reel contains copyrighted music, your app can find royalty-free Sound Collection tracks to replace it'. New 'media_audio_type' = 'MUSIC (licensed music from Meta's catalog) or ORIGINAL_SOUND'. Copyright detection: 'The media_url field is omitted from responses if the media contains copyrighted material'; actions 'BLOCK' / 'MUTE'; 'We only support Instagram media created via the content publishing API for early copyright detection.' The IG User Media reference still lists only 'audio_name' ('For Reels only. Name of the audio of your Reels media'); the container parameter for an ig_audio id was not found.

findings.claim: In Australia, an APRA AMCOS/OneMusic licence covers in-shop public performance only; it does not give the barber the right to put commercial chart music into social videos.
findings.evidence: APRA FAQ: its licence 'does not extend to uploading videos with music to social media, and additional permission from copyright holder(s) is generally required'; 'APRA AMCOS does not issue licences that give creators the right to place music into videos' (those rights sit with publishers and record companies); platform licences 'DO NOT cover "synchronisations" made for commercial purposes'. OneMusic: 'personal/non-commercial use of music in social media videos is covered under our agreements with the social media platforms' and suggests 'production or royalty-free music' for business videos.

findings.claim: Storyblocks offers a developer API with free test keys, but production keys and licensing are negotiated through enterprise sales; downloads via a production key are licensed for end users.
findings.evidence: Developer portal: test keys 'restricted to internal use, solely for testing purposes, and will have lower limits than full access keys'; full access keys come from 'API Sales at enterprise@storyblocks.com'; HMAC auth with public and secret key; limits 'vary for each client as they are formulated in the agreement with Storyblocks'. Marketing: a production API licence includes the full library and 'every download comes fully licensed, so your users are covered from day one'; Business licence 'royalty-free, worldwide in perpetuity' with '$1 million in indemnification'.

findings.claim: Shutterstock's public API documents audio search and licensing endpoints usable with an ordinary API subscription (status in 2025-2026 not confirmed).
findings.evidence: API reference: audio search with genre/instrument/mood/BPM filters; 'POST /v2/audio/licenses' licenses up to 50 tracks, 'The download links in the response are valid for 8 hours'; sandbox licensing returns 'a preset sample file'. Getting started: the API 'works with images, video clips, and music tracks for all Shutterstock subscriptions'; 'Get a free or paid API subscription'. Library values include 'shutterstock', 'premier', 'premiumbeat'. No 2024-2025 deprecation notice found, but docs are old (SDK ~629 days).

findings.claim: Pond5's API is partner-only with negotiated terms and no public documentation.
findings.evidence: 'The Pond5 API powers resellers, marketing affiliates, and other distribution partners across the globe'; Pond5 'customizes licensing rights, pricing terms, and content selection to meet your specific needs'; music 'must be incorporated into a production and cannot be sold or distributed as the original file'.

findings.claim: AI-music APIs are the only truly self-serve, pay-as-you-go option, but their commercial scopes are inconsistently stated: ElevenLabs Music API is $0.15/min with commercial use on Starter+ plans; Mubert's sublicensing tier is contradictory; Soundraw API starts at $29.99/month.
findings.evidence: ElevenLabs API pricing: 'Music Generation at $0.15 per minute, with a 5 minute duration limit and commercial use licensing on Starter+ plans'; Music API page: 'broad commercial use on all paid plans. Film, TV, and large studio game rights require an Enterprise plan', but the /api page says music 'requires an additional license for advertising, film, TV, games, and enterprise distribution'. Mubert: Trial '$49 and $99 per month' (100 generations), Startup '$199 and $249 per month' (5,000), Startup+ '$499'; blog: sublicensing 'allowing end-users to export content containing Mubert music and post it on social media, is only available on the Startup+ plan and above' while another Mubert page says 'Startup Plan includes sub-licensing'; 'registering tracks in Content ID is not allowed on any plan'. Soundraw: 'API Starter plan is listed at $29.99/month for up to 100 songs/month', 'API Pro plan is listed at $300/month for up to 1000 songs/month with a 6-month minimum commitment'.

implementation_decision:
Decision for Studio Assistant: build a provider-agnostic 'Licensed Catalogue' whose source of truth is owner-uploaded tracks plus a per-track licence record ('licence passport'), and treat any provider API as an optional adapter that writes into the same model. Do NOT build the product around a library API: Epidemic Sound (partnership agreement + Order Form; free plan is prototyping-only, 50 downloads, no commercial licence) and Artlist (Enterprise-only Music API) are unrealistic for a one-shop app; Uppbeat's API is unreleased; Musicbed, Pixabay (audio), YouTube Audio Library and FMA have no API; Freesound's API needs a negotiated licence for commercial use; ccMixter's Query API is CC-only. 

Phase 1 (ship now): (1) Owner buys ONE business-eligible subscription in the shop's legal/trading name and downloads tracks manually; Studio Assistant stores the files and the licence passport. Shortlist by cost/coverage for an Ivanhoe barber posting organic Reels/TikToks with occasional boosts: Soundstripe Business (US$999/yr; paid social 'local audience') or Pro (US$239/yr; 'commercial content created by individuals, including client projects and digital ads' - confirm with Soundstripe that a sole-trader shop's own brand content qualifies), Epidemic Sound Commercial (publish 'anywhere online', digital ads, one user, business turnover cap), Uppbeat Business (US$34.99/mo yearly) or Pro (US$14.99/mo yearly), Artlist Pro/Max Business (never the Social plan), Musicbed Business (~US$99.99/mo). Free/CC sources allowed only as CC BY or CC0 (Pixabay, Incompetech CC BY, ccMixter lic=by/CC0, Freesound CC0/CC BY downloaded manually), never CC BY-NC, YouTube Audio Library standard-licence tracks, TikTok CML or Meta Sound Collection audio in exported MP4s. (2) Licence passport schema on music_tracks: provider (enum incl. owner_upload), provider_track_id/url, title, artist, duration/bpm/mood, licence_type (subscription | single_track | cc_by | cc_by_sa | cc0 | platform_only | standard_paid), licence_holder (business name), licence_account_email, plan_name, licence_ref_or_code (e.g. Uppbeat credit code, Epidemic track licence, Tribe of Noise certificate), purchased_at, licence_document_asset (PDF/receipt/screenshot upload), download_record_asset (Pixabay-style proof), permitted_platforms[] (instagram, facebook, tiktok, youtube, website, email, in_store), permitted_use_types[] (organic_social, paid_social, client_work), territory, term_type (perpetual_for_published_projects | requires_active_subscription | one_project), valid_until (nullable), attribution_required (bool), attribution_text (exact string to paste), claim_clearance_notes (safelisted channels / claim-release instructions / Content ID shield flag), prohibited_uses (free text), verified_by, verified_at. (3) Enforcement in the renderer/export flow: a track is selectable only if licence passport is complete and verified; export to a platform not in permitted_platforms is blocked (not just warned); if attribution_required, the caption draft auto-includes attribution_text and the publish step requires an 'attribution included' confirmation; tracks with valid_until < today or term_type requires_active_subscription and a lapsed-subscription flag are quarantined for new renders (existing published exports remain, matching Soundstripe/Epidemic wording); platform_only tracks are never rendered into MP4s. (4) Usage ledger music_usage_log: track_id, render_id/export_id, destination platforms, post_url, posted_at, caption snapshot, attribution_included, and an immutable JSON snapshot of the licence passport at time of use - this is the evidence pack if Rights Manager/Content ID/TikTok disputes a post. (5) Platform-native audio path: offer a 'music-free export' (dialogue/ambient only, normalised) so the owner can add TikTok Commercial Sounds or Meta Sound Collection audio inside the apps where those licences are valid; record that choice in the ledger as platform_native_audio. If Studio Assistant publishes to TikTok via the Content Posting API, render the mandated line 'By posting, you agree to TikTok's Music Usage Confirmation' before the publish button and keep the owner's confirmation in the ledger. For Instagram API publishing, poll the container's copyright status before publishing and surface BLOCK/MUTE results. 

Phase 2 (optional provider adapter): define a MusicProvider interface (search, preview URL, acquire/download with licence metadata, licence snapshot) and implement one adapter only when the owner has an account that makes it worthwhile: first candidate Soundstripe (self-serve 30-day trial key for development; production key via sales; serve previews from Soundstripe CDN; keep the key server-side), second Storyblocks (free test keys; production via enterprise sales), third Shutterstock audio API (ordinary API subscription; verify endpoints are still live). An AI-music adapter (ElevenLabs Music API at US$0.15/min, Starter+ plan) is a cheap 'generate a bed' fallback but gate it behind confirmation of advertising rights in current ElevenLabs terms. Phase 3 (watch): adopt the Instagram Audio API (June 2026) to attach Sound Collection tracks server-side once the container parameter is confirmed and the Facebook-Login app has passed app review. Tell the owner plainly in the UI that no chart/trending music can be baked into exported files, and that in-shop OneMusic/APRA licences do not cover social videos.
account_requirements: Owner: purchase one business-eligible music subscription in the business's name (Soundstripe Pro/Business, Epidemic Sound Commercial, Uppbeat Pro/Business, Artlist Pro/Max Business, or Musicbed Business). Personal/Social/Creator tiers (Epidemic Personal, Artlist Social, Musicbed Personal, Soundstripe Personal, Uppbeat Free) do not cover brand/promotional content or paid social. Keep invoices and the licence certificate/receipt for each downloaded track for upload into the licence passport.

Owner: register/safelist the shop's YouTube channel, Instagram, Facebook Page and TikTok account in the chosen provider's clearance tool (Epidemic safelisting, Soundstripe claim clearance/single-use codes, Uppbeat Claim Release) so Content ID/Rights Manager do not claim or mute posts; record safelisted channels in claim_clearance_notes.

Owner: confirm with the provider (support ticket, keep the reply) that their plan covers (a) organic posts on the business's own Instagram/Facebook/TikTok/YouTube, (b) the shop's website, and (c) boosted/paid social if used; paid social is excluded on Soundstripe Personal, limited to a 'local audience' on Soundstripe Business, and capped at US$5,000 ad spend on Musicbed subscriptions.

Owner (TikTok): keep the TikTok Business Account - only Commercial Sounds are offered in-app and the general library is personal/non-commercial. CML tracks may only be used on TikTok; never export them into MP4s for Instagram/YouTube/website.

Owner (Instagram/Facebook): business accounts may lack the Licensed Music Library in Australia; use Meta Sound Collection or original audio in-app for Reels/boosts/ads. Sound Collection audio is licensed only on Meta products - never bake it into exported files.

Owner (Australia): a OneMusic/APRA AMCOS licence for in-shop music does not cover synchronising commercial music into social videos; sync rights come from publishers/labels and are not provided by OneMusic.

Developer, if posting to TikTok via Content Posting API: pass TikTok's client audit (unaudited clients can only post privately, 5 users/24h); display 'By posting, you agree to TikTok's Music Usage Confirmation' before the publish button; honour per-account posting caps.

Developer, if publishing Reels via Instagram Content Publishing API: Meta app review for instagram_content_publish (and Facebook Login + relevant permissions if using the June 2026 Instagram Audio API); video_url must be publicly reachable; check container copyright status before media_publish; 100 API posts per 24h limit.

Developer, if building a Soundstripe adapter: self-serve 30-day trial API key (watermarked previews) for development; production key and end-user licence terms require a Soundstripe sales/enterprise agreement; API key must stay server-side; content served via Soundstripe CDN.
Developer, if building a Storyblocks adapter: free test keys for internal testing only; production keys and licence via enterprise@storyblocks.com (HMAC public/secret key auth).

Developer, if building a Shutterstock adapter: Shutterstock developer account with a free or paid API subscription; confirm audio endpoints (GET /v2/audio/search, POST /v2/audio/licenses) are still live before committing.

Developer, if using Epidemic Sound Partner API: partnership agreement + Order Form + Acceptable Use Policy; Free plan is prototyping-only (50 downloads, no commercial licence, no safelisting); end users need their own paid Epidemic subscription via ES Connect for a commercial licence.
Developer, if using Artlist Music API: Enterprise plan (custom pricing) is mandatory; standard plans cannot be sublicensed or embedded in an app.

Developer, if using Freesound API in a commercial product: negotiate a commercial API licence with UPF; respect per-user limits (60/min, 2,000/day); use only CC0/CC BY sounds and generate attribution for CC BY.

Developer, if using an AI-music API (ElevenLabs Music, Mubert, Soundraw): paid plan with explicit commercial/sublicensing rights (ElevenLabs Starter+ at US$0.15/min; Mubert sublicensing tier is ambiguous - confirm in writing); record the generation ID and licence certificate per track; note Mubert bans Content ID registration.

Operational: for every CC BY track (Incompetech, ccMixter, Pixabay optional credit, Uppbeat free) the exact attribution string must be stored and auto-inserted in captions; CC BY-NC tracks must be rejected at import.
uncertainties: No official page could be read in full: every target host (epidemicsound.com, developers.epidemicsound.com, soundstripe.com, docs.soundstripe.com, artlist.io, uppbeat.io, musicbed.com, pixabay.com, freesound.org, freemusicarchive.org, ccmixter.org, incompetech.com, support.google.com, tiktok.com, ads.tiktok.com, facebook.com) returned ENOTFOUND in this sandbox; all quotes come from WebSearch extended-mode summaries of those pages and should be re-verified against the live pages before the owner buys anything.

Prices conflict across sources for Epidemic Sound (Personal US$9.99-15/mo, Commercial US$19-49.99/mo depending on source), Uppbeat (Pro US$12.99-24.99), Artlist (Social US$9.99-14.99) and Musicbed; Soundstripe's help-centre prices (Personal US$119/yr, Pro US$239/yr, Pro Plus US$399/yr, Business US$999/yr) looked current but are not confirmed, and AUD pricing/GST was not checked.

Epidemic Sound: whether productions published during a Commercial subscription remain cleared after cancellation was not confirmed from the licence text (only 'use ... until your next renewal period' billing wording was found); Soundstripe explicitly keeps past projects licensed.

Soundstripe API end-user licence model (whether a single platform licence covers all end users' downloads or each user needs a subscription) and production API pricing are not public; Storyblocks and Shutterstock API pricing likewise unknown; whether Shutterstock's audio/PremiumBeat endpoints are still active in 2026 was not confirmed.

Instagram Audio API (June 1, 2026): the parameter for attaching an ig_audio id when creating a Reels container was not found (reference still lists only audio_name); availability to Instagram-Login-only apps and app-review scopes unconfirmed.

Whether Australian Instagram business accounts currently get the Licensed Music Library is not documented in any captured official page; Meta only says access depends on 'account type' and 'country or region'. Third-party claims about a 'Meta Soundtrack+' tier or 2023-2025 licensed-music-for-business rollouts were not verifiable.

YouTube Audio Library: official text does not state whether standard-licence tracks may be used in videos posted off YouTube; third-party guides claim standard-licence tracks are YouTube-only while CC tracks may be used anywhere with credit. Treat standard-licence tracks as YouTube-only until YouTube confirms.

TikTok CML 'Usable Placements' are per track and only visible in the web CML; the current version date of the CML User Terms and Music Terms (EEA variants were the ones found) was not visible; Business Terms wording about clearing rights yourself came from a summary.
Incompetech Standard License price (reported US$30/one song, US$50/two, US$20 each for three or more) is from third-party sites, not the official page; CC version (3.0 vs 4.0) varies by track.
ccMixter 'dig-lic=safe' commercial filter is from a 2013 forum post; 'Tunetrack' (ccMixter's reported paid-licensing arm) returned no results and is unverified.
Freesound: commercial API licence pricing with UPF is case-by-case and not published; the 2023 report referenced is ~1.4 years old.
Uppbeat: free-plan download caps (3 vs 10 per month), the 'perpetual licence' vs 'active subscription' wording, and API release timing conflict across sources.

ElevenLabs Music API: ElevenLabs' own pages contradict each other on whether advertising use is included on paid plans or needs an additional licence; Merlin/Kobalt catalogue partnerships could not be confirmed. Mubert's sublicensing tier (Startup vs Startup+) is contradicted on Mubert's own pages. Copyright status of AI-generated music under Australian law (and hence enforceability/exclusivity) was not researched.
Musicbed: no API found via site-restricted search, but absence of evidence is not proof; Pond5 API is partner-only with no public docs.

Whether the Meta 'Access to the licensed music library on Instagram' Business Help page (business/help/402084904469945) enumerates business-account eligibility is unknown - its body text was not captured.

findings.claim: Spam Act consent can be express or inferred; the Act's Schedule 2 defines consent as express consent or consent reasonably inferred from conduct and the business/other relationships.
findings.evidence: Search summary of the 2005 compilation of the Spam Act, Schedule 2: consent means '(a) express consent; or (b) consent that can reasonably be inferred from: (i) the conduct; and (ii) the business and other relationships'. ACMA guidance: 'inferred consent is generally when a person has a provable, ongoing relationship with your business, and the marketing is directly related to that relationship' and inferred consent is 'less common and reliable than express consent'.

findings.claim: A one-off purchase, an email enquiry, an email given only for a receipt, or a past (ended) customer relationship does NOT establish inferred consent; the burden of proving consent is on the sender; you cannot email someone to ask for consent.
findings.evidence: ACMA (search summaries): businesses have misunderstood the rules by adding people 'on the apparent basis of a one-off purchase, or where the consumer has simply submitted an email enquiry'; where shoppers give an email address only to receive a receipt, that 'does not meet the requirements of consent'; 'it is always preferable to obtain a consumer's express consent'; 'it's up to you to prove that you have a person's consent'. ACMA SpinTel release (Nov 2026): SpinTel 'paid a $653,400 penalty after sending more than 32,000 commercial emails without consent' to former customers; ACMA said 'a previous business relationship did not automatically provide consent to send marketing messages'. Secondary (Corrs, attributing ACMA): 'You cannot send an electronic message to ask for consent, because this is a marketing message.'

findings.claim: Every commercial electronic message must identify the sender and include contact details (Spam Act s 17), and this applies even to designated (factual) messages.
findings.evidence: ACMA: a message must contain content that 'identifies you as the sender; contains your contact details; makes it easy to unsubscribe'. Legislation summary: designated commercial electronic messages 'are exempt from section 16 ... and section 18' but 'Sender identification still applies under section 17'. ACMA: exempt organisations 'must still include their contact details in the message'.

findings.claim: Unsubscribe facility rules: clear instructions, actioned within 5 working/business days, no fee or premium cost, functional for at least 30 days after sending, no login/account creation and no extra personal information beyond the address being unsubscribed.
findings.evidence: ACMA fact sheet (May 2024): the unsubscribe option 'has clear instructions on how to unsubscribe, is actioned within 5 working days, does not charge a fee, and works for at least 30 days after the message was sent'; senders 'cannot ask you to log into an account or provide personal information to unsubscribe (other than the email or phone number to be unsubscribed) unless you've agreed in advance'. ACMA investigation report: 'Clause 6 of Schedule 2 to the Spam Act states that withdrawal of consent takes effect at the end of the period of 5 business days'. Spam Act s 18 (AustLII summary): the unsubscribe address must be reasonably likely to receive the unsubscribe message and similar messages 'at all times during a period of at least 30 days after the message is sent'; older compilation text: 'the statement is presented in a clear and conspicuous manner'. Spam Regulations 2021 ES: use of the address 'must not require the recipient ... to use a premium service' and 'must not cost more than the usual cost'; regulations in force 'from 1 April 2021'. ACMA (Kogan matter) treated a facility that 'was not simple and easy to unsubscribe' as non-functional.

findings.claim: Factual-only messages (e.g. a pure appointment reminder/confirmation) are 'designated commercial electronic messages' exempt from the consent (s 16) and unsubscribe (s 18) requirements, but any promotional content or links to promotional pages makes the message commercial, and ACMA actively enforces this.
findings.evidence: Spam Act Schedule 1 (summary): a designated commercial electronic message is one 'consisting of no more than factual information, with or without directly related comment, plus the name, logo and contact details of whoever authorised it'; such messages 'are exempt from section 16 ... and section 18'. ACMA Ticketek (Oct 2023): emails 'linked to Ticketek's website and social media pages, which contained advertising material and promotions', so 'one of the purposes of the message was also to advertise and promote goods and services, so the messages were not designated'; $500,000 penalty. ACMA DoorDash (Aug 2023): messages 'mischaracterised ... as being solely factual' because a footer banner promoted jobs; $2,011,320; ACMA's count excluded 'Notifications + Reminders, Account Messages, Order Confirmation Message, Support - Transactional'. Lululemon (secondary report of ACMA notice, 8 Dec 2025, $702,900): ACMA 'rejected the argument that the emails were mostly factual'. Corrs: 'It is not enough to simply characterise an electronic message to customers as "factual" or "transactional" to avoid the spam rules.' Appointment-reminder exemption specifically is stated only by a law-firm blog, not by ACMA.

findings.claim: Review/feedback requests should be treated as commercial electronic messages (consent + unsubscribe required); withdrawal of consent must be honoured exactly as given.
findings.evidence: Secondary (Corrs/Dynamic Business, attributing ACMA): 'The ACMA also considers surveys and free offer type promotions to fall within the Spam Act as they have a commercial intent.' No ACMA page found that rules on review requests specifically. ACMA TAB (Jul 2026, $2.7m): breaches involved customers 'who had withdrawn their consent to receiving marketing via a specific channel, but had not opted out of all marketing'; ACMA has 'not been sympathetic to businesses which have made a genuine mistake or experienced a technical error that resulted in commercial electronic messages being sent ... after they had made an unsubscribe request.'

findings.claim: No amendment to the Spam Act 2003 or Spam Regulations 2021 was found for 2024-2026; the change in this period is enforcement intensity (ACMA 2025-26 priority; penalties: Lululemon Dec 2025 $702,900; Latitude Apr 2026 $3.96m; TAB Jul 2026 $2.7m; SpinTel Nov 2026 $653,400).
findings.evidence: Searches for 2024-2026 amendments returned only the 2006 review ('the Act was operating successfully and should not be amended') and the 2021 Regulations. ACMA: 'in 2025-26 the ACMA focused on persistent unwanted spam or telemarketing'; TAB release: 'businesses have paid more than $12 million in penalties for spam and telemarketing breaches over the past 18 months'. Latitude: 'paid a $3.96 million penalty after the ACMA found the company breached Australia's spam laws more than 2.7 million times' (15 April 2026).

findings.claim: Resend pricing (Nov 2026): Free $0 = 3,000 emails/month capped at 100/day, 3 domains, 30-day retention, 1 webhook endpoint, 1,000 marketing contacts; Pro $20/month = 50,000 emails, 10 domains, no daily limit, 5 webhook endpoints, overage $0.90/1,000; Scale $90/month = 100,000 emails, 1,000 domains, 10 webhook endpoints; dedicated IP $30/month on Scale; rate limit 10 requests/second per team.
findings.evidence: resend.com/pricing summary: 'Free Recommended $0 / mo 3,000 emails / mo' with 'a cap of 100 emails per day'; 'Pro $20 / mo, 50,000 emails / mo, 10 domains, No daily email limit, 5 webhook endpoints'; 'Scale $90 / mo, 100,000 emails / mo, 1,000 domains, 10 webhook endpoints'; Free plan 'includes one webhook endpoint' and 'all events are available on every plan'; 'Free $0/mo 1,000 contacts'. Knowledge base: 'Resend retains email data for 30 days across all plans (Free, Pro, and Scale)'; 'The default maximum rate limit is 10 requests per second per team'; over-quota sends 'return a 429 with daily_quota_exceeded or monthly_quota_exceeded' and are not queued or retried.

findings.claim: Resend has no Australian region and no data residency outside the US: sending regions are us-east-1, eu-west-1, sa-east-1, ap-northeast-1 (Tokyo nearest to Australia); all account data is stored in the United States regardless of region.
findings.evidence: Resend regions doc: users 'can send ... from North Virginia (us-east-1), Ireland (eu-west-1), São Paulo (sa-east-1), and Tokyo (ap-northeast-1)'; 'Account data, including email metadata, logs, and API records, is stored in the United States regardless of the sending region'; changelog: 'free users can now send emails from any region'. Create Domain API lists only those four region values.

findings.claim: Resend one-click unsubscribe: Broadcasts automatically add List-Unsubscribe/List-Unsubscribe-Post headers and a per-recipient {{{RESEND_UNSUBSCRIBE_URL}}} link; for transactional API sends you must add both headers yourself and host the RFC 8058 POST endpoint.
findings.evidence: Resend docs: Resend 'doesn't manage contact lists for transactional email', you 'pass the List-Unsubscribe header through the API'; bulk messages need 'a URL-form List-Unsubscribe header plus List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click'; the endpoint 'should return 200 or 202 to a POST and must stop sending within 48 hours'; the docs' Node example sets only List-Unsubscribe. Broadcasts: 'We also include the proper unsubscribe headers automatically, according to Gmail and Yahoo's bulk sending requirements'; unsubscribed contacts 'will be skipped when sending the next Broadcast'; contacts have an 'unsubscribed' flag meaning unsubscribed 'from all Broadcasts'.

findings.claim: Resend webhooks cover delivered/bounced/complained and more (email.sent, email.delivered, email.delivery_delayed, email.failed, email.opened, email.clicked, email.bounced, email.complained, email.received, email.scheduled, email.suppressed, contact.*, domain.*, suppression.added/removed), signed with svix headers and verifiable via resend.webhooks.verify; Resend auto-suppresses hard-bounced and complained addresses across transactional and Broadcast sends, with a suppressions API (bulk up to 100).
findings.evidence: Resend docs: event list as above; 'The request carries svix-id, svix-timestamp, and svix-signature headers'; 'resend.webhooks.verify ... throws on an invalid request'; 'The raw request body must be used for verification'. Suppressions doc: an address is added 'for one of three reasons: a permanent bounce, a spam complaint, or a manual addition'; it 'is skipped across all your domains and subdomains when sending transactional or Broadcast emails'; a suppressed send 'fires an email.suppressed webhook'; 'bulk suppress up to 100 at a time using the API'; 'Not all Inbox Service Providers return a complained event, most notably, Gmail/Google Workspace'.

findings.claim: Resend batch API: resend.batch.send([...]) up to 100 emails per request, whole batch rejected if any email is invalid, no attachments, tags supported; Node SDK is npm package 'resend' (github resend/resend-node).
findings.evidence: Batch doc: 'caps each request at 100 emails'; 'The request will fail and return an error if any email in your payload is invalid'; 'the attachments field is not supported yet'; changelog: tags 'now works' on emails/batch. Node docs: 'npm install resend'; API key via RESEND_API_KEY; 'resend.emails.send()' returns data or error.

findings.claim: Postmark pricing (Nov 2026): Free developer plan 100 emails/month (no overages, no expiry); Basic $15/month = 10,000 emails, 45-day retention, 5 custom sending domains, up to 4 users/5 servers/15 streams, overage $1.80/1,000; Pro $16.50/month = 10,000 emails, retention up to 365 days, 10 domains, 6 users/10 servers/30 streams, inbound email, overage $1.30/1,000; Platform $18/month = unlimited domains, overage $1.20/1,000; dedicated IP $50/month (Pro+, 300k+/month senders); monthly billing only.
findings.evidence: postmarkapp.com/pricing and pricing.txt summaries: 'all new accounts start off on our free developer plan with 100 emails per month'; Free 'does not allow overages' and 'has no expiration date'; Basic 'includes 45-day data retention, 5 custom sending domains' and 'up to 4 users, up to 5 servers, up to 15 streams'; Pro 'customizable data retention up to 365 days (45-day default), 10 custom sending domains', 'up to 6 users, up to 10 servers, up to 30 streams'; Platform 'unlimited custom sending domains'; overages '$1.80, $1.30, and $1.20 per 1,000'; dedicated IPs 'Starting at $50/month per IP ... only available on Pro plans or higher' for '300,000 emails per month or more'; 'Postmark offers monthly billing plans only'.

findings.claim: Postmark stores all data in the United States (Deft data centre near Chicago plus AWS) with no EU/AU region planned; cross-border basis is SCCs/DPF.
findings.evidence: Postmark GDPR FAQ: Postmark 'is a US-based company and also stores its data in the US, including personal data of its customers'; EU privacy page: 'doesn't have plans to add servers in the EU'; 'The primary data and servers sit at Deft's data center (located outside of Chicago) and Amazon Web Services (AWS)'; 'All sent email messages are stored on Postmark servers for 45 days by default'.

findings.claim: Postmark Broadcast message streams automatically add an RFC 8058 one-click unsubscribe (List-Unsubscribe + List-Unsubscribe-Post headers) and an unsubscribe link ({{{ pm:unsubscribe }}} placeholder, appended if omitted); unsubscribes are per stream; transactional streams don't require unsubscribe but pass through custom headers; promotional mail through a Transactional stream gets sending paused.
findings.evidence: Postmark: it 'automatically adds a one-click unsubscribe link to the bottom of every message sent through a Broadcast Message Stream' and 'adds the List-Unsubscribe-Post and List-Unsubscribe headers to messages that follow RFC 8058'; 'there is not a way to edit the List-Unsubscribe headers' while Postmark manages them; placeholder '{{{ pm:unsubscribe }}} ... If you leave it out, Postmark adds it at the end of the message'; self-managed unsubscribes 'requires approval'; 'If a recipient unsubscribes from a broadcast stream email, you can still send to them through your transactional stream'; 'If you add Unsubscribe headers to transactional messages, Postmark will include them in your send'; 'If Postmark detects promotional email going through a Transactional Stream, sending is paused.'

findings.claim: Postmark exposes per-stream suppression lists (reasons HardBounce, SpamComplaint, ManualSuppression; origins Recipient, Customer, Admin), a Suppressions API (dump, create up to 50 addresses/call, delete except SpamComplaint), and a SubscriptionChange webhook that fires on add/remove with SuppressSending; webhook record types include Delivery, Bounce, SpamComplaint, Open, Click, SubscriptionChange.
findings.evidence: Suppressions API summary: filters 'by HardBounce, SpamComplaint, ManualSuppression, and by origin, which takes Recipient, Customer, Admin'; 'Creation accepts up to 50 addresses per call'; 'SpamComplaint suppressions cannot be deleted'; 'Deleting a HardBounce suppression is the equivalent of reactivating the associated Bounce'. Subscription change webhook: 'fires when an address is added to or removed from a stream's suppression list'; 'The SuppressSending field will inform whether that was a deactivation or reactivation'; 'if a recipient unsubscribes, they will be suppressed with the SuppressionReason of ManualSuppression'.

findings.claim: Postmark batch endpoint accepts up to 500 messages per call (50 MB), each validated/sent independently; official Node library is npm 'postmark' (github ActiveCampaign/postmark.js, v5.x, Node 18+), using ServerClient for sending.
findings.evidence: Batch docs: 'The batch endpoint accepts up to 500 messages per API call, and up to 50 MB payload size, including attachments'; 'Each message in the batch is validated and sent independently'; 'A released message can still bounce or be deferred after it leaves Postmark'. Libraries page/npm: 'npm i postmark'; 'ServerClient handles sending email, bounces, templates, stats, webhooks, and streams'; 'The current version (5.1.1 on npm) needs Node 18 or later'.

findings.claim: Postmark requires manual account approval before you can email recipients outside your own domain (HTTP 412 'Account Pending Approval'), and its Broadcast policy requires explicit opt-in (e.g. a checked box), bans purchased/acquired lists, and expects complaint rate < 0.1% and bounces < 10%.
findings.evidence: API overview: error 412 is returned 'when an account is pending approval and recipients aren't on the sender's domain'; approval via 'Request approval button in the dashboard', typically about 24 hours (third-party reports). Postmark guidance: 'treating a Terms of Service agreement as permission' is out; 'Recipients must take an action, such as checking a box, to opt in'; customers wanting to send to 'purchased, free, acquired, or cross-branded lists are not a good fit'; 'spam complaint rate must stay below 0.1% with bounces below 10%'; 'Recipients should have been contacted, or have opted in, within the past 3 months' (older guidance).

findings.claim: Gmail sender guidelines: all senders need SPF or DKIM; bulk senders (~5,000+/day to personal Gmail, permanently thereafter) need SPF+DKIM+DMARC (min p=none) and RFC 8058 one-click unsubscribe (List-Unsubscribe HTTPS URL + 'List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click') on marketing/promotional mail, honoured within 48 hours/2 days; keep Postmaster Tools spam rate below 0.10% and never reach 0.30%; enforcement ramped with temporary and permanent rejections (latest milestone 'November 2025').
findings.evidence: Google summaries: 'All senders: SPF or DKIM. Bulk senders: SPF, DKIM, and DMARC'; 'Senders who meet the above criteria at least once are permanently considered bulk senders'; 'To meet our one-click unsubscribe requirement, you must use List-Unsubscribe email headers in all commercial, promotional messages, as described in RFC 8058'; 'mailto and URL unsubscribe links don't meet our one-click unsubscribe requirement'; 'Transactional messages are excluded'; 'Process and honor unsubscribe requests within 48 hours'; 'keep spam rates reported in Postmaster Tools below 0.10% and avoid ever reaching a spam rate of 0.30% or higher'; 'Gmail is ramping up its enforcement on non-compliant traffic ... including temporary and permanent rejections'; Google 'doesn't automatically reject messages' solely for missing one-click, but such senders are ineligible for mitigation.

findings.claim: Yahoo sender requirements mirror Gmail: SPF and DKIM, DMARC at least p=none with (relaxed) alignment, DKIM key >= 1024 bits (2048 recommended), RFC 8058 one-click unsubscribe (POST 'highly recommended') for marketing/subscribed mail honoured within 2 days, complaint rate below 0.3% (measured on inbox-delivered mail via the Complaint Feedback Loop), valid forward/reverse DNS, RFC 5321/5322 compliance; Microsoft Outlook.com added SPF/DKIM/DMARC requirements for 5,000+/day senders from 5 May 2025.
findings.evidence: Yahoo Sender Hub summary: 'We require a DKIM key length of 1024 bits or greater'; DMARC 'at minimum p=none that passes'; 'Requests must be honored within 2 days'; 'one-click unsubscribe is only required for promotional/marketing messages'; 'spam rate is calculated in our system based on mail delivered to the inbox'. Microsoft: 'Outlook.com began enforcing these standards starting May 5th, 2025'; 'DMARC needs at least p=none and alignment with either SPF or DKIM'; no List-Unsubscribe mandate found for Outlook.

findings.claim: Privacy Act 1988 likely does not bind a barber with annual turnover of $3M or less (small business exemption), so APP 8 cross-border rules on using US-hosted Postmark/Resend are not legally triggered, though reforms recommend removing the exemption.
findings.evidence: OAIC: 'A small business is one with an annual turnover of $3 million or less'; exceptions include businesses that 'provide a health service and hold health information' or 'trade in personal information'; OAIC 'recommends that all businesses, regardless of size and activity, are covered by the Privacy Act' but no source confirms enactment; from 10 December 2026 privacy policies must note automated decisions (tranche 1).

implementation_decision:
PROVIDER: Use Postmark (Basic plan, USD $15/month, 10,000 emails) as the primary provider, behind an `EmailProvider` adapter interface with Resend as the documented fallback. Reasons: (1) at a barber's volume (likely < 3,000/month) Resend Free is $0 but its 100 emails/day cap would spread a single campaign to a few hundred clients over several days, and Resend Pro ($20) costs more than Postmark Basic ($15); (2) Postmark gives provider-enforced compliance primitives the app can audit: separate Transactional and Broadcast message streams, automatic RFC 8058 one-click headers and unsubscribe link on the Broadcast stream (no need to build and risk-break our own one-click endpoint, which is exactly what ACMA fined Lululemon for), per-stream suppression lists with a Suppressions API and a SubscriptionChange webhook, batch sends of 500, 45-day message retention, npm `postmark` (ServerClient). (3) Neither provider offers an Australian region or AU data residency (Resend: 4 sending regions, nearest Tokyo, account data in the US; Postmark: US only). Accept US hosting, disclose it in the privacy notice. Use the Resend adapter only if Postmark approval is refused (then Resend Free for transactional + Pro $20 when campaigns need > 100/day; on Resend we must add both List-Unsubscribe headers ourselves on API sends and host the one-click POST endpoint, or use Resend Broadcasts/Segments which store contacts at Resend).

MESSAGE CLASSES (hard-coded in the app, one enum, enforced by a template linter):
- `transactional_factual` (booking confirmation, reminder, reschedule/cancellation notice, receipt): Postmark Transactional stream; content limited to facts + business name/contact details (Spam Act s 17 still applies); NO offers, discount codes, 'book your next visit' CTAs, social/promo links (Ticketek/DoorDash/Lululemon precedent). No consent needed and no Spam Act unsubscribe required, but keep a product-level 'reminders off' preference. Linter blocks promotional phrases and any link outside the booking-management page.
- `review_request` and `campaign`: treated as commercial electronic messages (conservative; ACMA treats surveys/free-offer messages as commercial): Postmark Broadcast stream only; require current consent; footer must contain business trading name, Ivanhoe VIC street address, phone, email, and the `{{{ pm:unsubscribe }}}` link; Postmark adds List-Unsubscribe/List-Unsubscribe-Post automatically. Max one review request per completed appointment, never to a suppressed/unsubscribed address.

DATA MODEL (Postgres):
1. `clients.email` (citext, normalised) + `clients.email_marketing_state` cached enum ('no_consent','express','inferred','withdrawn','suppressed').
2. `email_consents` (append-only ledger): id, client_id, email_snapshot, scope ('marketing' = campaigns + review requests; single scope so one unsubscribe withdraws all commercial email, per the TAB finding), status ('express'|'inferred'|'withdrawn'), method ('booking_form_checkbox'|'in_store_signup'|'website_form'|'verbal_recorded_by_staff'|'import_with_evidence'), consent_text (exact wording shown, unticked-by-default checkbox), evidence jsonb (form id/version, IP, user agent, timestamp, staff user id, attachment ref), granted_at, recorded_by, withdrawn_at, withdrawn_via ('one_click_post'|'link'|'reply'|'in_person'|'staff'|'provider_webhook'|'spam_complaint'). Rules: default and recommended state is `express`; `inferred` is allowed only for a client with >= 2 completed appointments in the last 12 months (app policy, not a statutory number) and auto-lapses to 'no_consent' when no completed appointment in 12 months; never email a client to request consent; 'verbal' consent is flagged as weak evidence in the UI.
3. `email_suppressions` (global, keyed by normalised email + scope): scope ('marketing'|'all'), reason ('unsubscribe'|'spam_complaint'|'hard_bounce'|'manual'|'invalid_address'), origin ('recipient'|'staff'|'provider'), provider_stream, provider_record_id, source_message_id, occurred_at, synced_to_provider_at. Hard bounce and spam complaint => scope 'all' (stop everything to that address); unsubscribe => scope 'marketing' (factual reminders continue, matching Postmark's per-stream model). Mirror both ways with Postmark: ingest SubscriptionChange (SuppressSending true/false) and Bounce/SpamComplaint webhooks; push staff-entered unsubscribes to the Broadcast stream via the Suppressions API (ManualSuppression, origin Customer) so Postmark also blocks them.
4. `email_messages` (send log, retained >= 24 months as compliance evidence; Postmark keeps only 45 days): id, client_id, to_email, message_class, stream, provider ('postmark'|'resend'), provider_message_id, campaign_id, template_key/version, subject, consent_id (FK to the consent relied on at send time), status ('queued','sent','delivered','delayed','bounced','complained','suppressed','failed'), timestamps per status.
5. `email_events` (raw webhook payloads, idempotent on provider MessageID + RecordType + ReceivedAt; webhook URL protected with HTTP basic auth + secret header; reject unknown record types gracefully).
6. `campaigns`: subject/body/template, audience_rule, scheduled_at, sent_at, counts, auto-pause thresholds.

SEND GATE (single function `assertCanSend(client, messageClass)` returning reason codes, called in the job worker, never bypassable from the UI): transactional_factual => email present, no 'all'-scope suppression, template passed factual linter. review_request/campaign => current consent in (express, inferred-and-not-lapsed), no suppression (any scope), Broadcast stream, footer identity block present, `{{{ pm:unsubscribe }}}` present, frequency cap honoured. Campaign sends use /email/batch in chunks of 500 with Promise.allSettled; record per-message results; auto-pause a campaign if complaints > 0.1% or bounces > 5% of delivered.

UNSUBSCRIBE HANDLING: process immediately (statutory maximum 5 business days; Gmail/Yahoo 48 hours/2 days): SubscriptionChange webhook => insert suppression + append 'withdrawn' consent row + update cached state within seconds; staff 'Unsubscribe' button for in-person/phone/reply requests does the same and calls the Suppressions API; the Reply-To is a monitored mailbox and the SOP says any reply saying unsubscribe/stop is actioned the same day. The unsubscribe facility must stay functional >= 30 days after each send (verify Postmark links do not expire; if self-managing, use a non-expiring HMAC token page that needs no login and asks for nothing but confirmation).

DOMAIN/AUTH: send only from the business's own domain (never @gmail.com From addresses): add Postmark DKIM TXT, custom Return-Path CNAME (SPF/DMARC alignment), SPF include for Postmark, DMARC `p=none` with rua reporting at launch, move to `p=quarantine` once reports are clean; register the domain in Google Postmaster Tools; keep complaint rate < 0.1%. One-click headers are strictly required by Gmail/Yahoo only for ~5,000+/day senders, but Postmark adds them on Broadcast anyway and they are good practice.
account_requirements: Own a domain for the business (not gmail.com) with DNS access: add Postmark DKIM TXT record, custom Return-Path CNAME, SPF include for Postmark, and a DMARC TXT record (minimum p=none; plan to move to p=quarantine).

Create a Postmark account (starts on the free developer plan, 100 emails/month, no overages, no expiry) and complete the manual 'Request approval' form describing the use case (appointment confirmations/reminders + opt-in marketing to existing clients); until approved, sends to recipients outside the business's own domain fail with HTTP 412 'Account Pending Approval' (typically reviewed in about 24 hours).

Upgrade Postmark to Basic (USD $15/month, 10,000 emails, 45-day retention, 5 domains, up to 4 users/5 servers/15 streams; overage $1.80 per 1,000) once live; choose Pro (USD $16.50/month) only if inbound email processing (reply handling) or retention up to 365 days is wanted. Monthly billing only; dedicated IP not needed.

Configure one Postmark server with a Transactional stream and a Broadcast stream; leave 'Manage Unsubscribes With Postmark' on for the Broadcast stream (self-managed unsubscribes require separate Postmark approval); set up webhooks for Delivery, Bounce, SpamComplaint and SubscriptionChange with basic-auth credentials.
Comply with Postmark's Broadcast policy: recipients must have explicitly opted in (e.g. a checked box), no purchased/acquired lists, keep spam complaints below 0.1% and bounces below 10%.

Spam Act obligations the owner must accept operationally: collect express consent (unticked checkbox at booking/in-store/website, exact wording kept) before any review request or campaign; never email people to ask for consent; every commercial email shows the business name and contact details; unsubscribes actioned within 5 business days (the app does it immediately) and the unsubscribe facility must work for at least 30 days; keep consent and unsubscribe records because the sender carries the burden of proof; honour in-person/phone/reply unsubscribe requests via the app's Unsubscribe action.
Register the sending domain in Google Postmaster Tools (requires SPF/DKIM to be passing) and watch the spam-rate dashboard (target < 0.10%, never 0.30%).

Publish a privacy notice stating that email delivery data is processed by Postmark (ActiveCampaign) in the United States; the Privacy Act small-business exemption (turnover <= $3M, no health-service/trading-in-personal-information exception) likely applies, but disclosure is still good practice.

Resend fallback account (only if Postmark approval is refused): verify the domain in Resend (Free: 3,000 emails/month, 100/day, 3 domains, 1 webhook endpoint, 30-day retention); Pro at USD $20/month removes the daily cap; on Resend the app must add List-Unsubscribe and List-Unsubscribe-Post headers itself and host the RFC 8058 POST endpoint, or use Resend Broadcasts/Segments.
uncertainties: Every official page (acma.gov.au, legislation.gov.au, austlii.edu.au, resend.com, postmarkapp.com, support.google.com, senders.yahooinc.com) was blocked by the sandbox network (DNS ENOTFOUND); all evidence is from WebSearch summaries of those pages, not full-page reads. The hosts must be allowed in the session's network settings for direct verification.

The exact current statutory wording of Spam Act s 18 and Schedule 2 clause 6 was not read verbatim; the '5 business days' figure rests on the ACMA fact sheet and an ACMA investigation report quoting clause 6, and the '30 days' figure on an AustLII s 18 summary. The latest compilation on legislation.gov.au could not be checked for amendments after 2021, though no 2024-2026 amendment was found.

Whether a bare review/feedback request is a 'commercial electronic message' has no ACMA ruling that I could find; the 'surveys have commercial intent' statement is attributed to ACMA by secondary law-firm sources. The design treats review requests as commercial to be safe.

Whether Postmark-hosted unsubscribe links expire (they must stay functional for at least 30 days after sending) was not confirmed in the pages found; verify with Postmark before go-live or add an app-hosted non-expiring unsubscribe page.

Postmark plan caps (users/servers/streams/domains per plan) came from a summary of postmarkapp.com/pricing.txt and may change; Platform-tier caps were not found. The '3 months recency' Broadcast guidance comes from older Postmark blog material. The postmark.js method name for batch sends (sendEmailBatch) was only seen in an old README; confirm against the current ServerClient API. Postmark webhook authentication options (basic auth/custom headers) were not verified in this session.

Resend's Free-plan details (3 domains, 30-day retention, 1 webhook endpoint, 1,000 contacts) are from 2026 summaries; Resend changed pricing several times in 2025-2026, so re-check before relying on them. One third-party source claimed received (inbound) emails count toward quota; unconfirmed.

Gmail/Yahoo enforcement status after the 'November 2025' ramp-up is unknown; the bulk-sender thresholds (~5,000/day) will not apply to this business, but the all-sender rules (authentication, low spam rate) do. Microsoft Outlook was not confirmed to require List-Unsubscribe.

The inferred-consent policy (>= 2 completed appointments in 12 months, lapsing after 12 months without a visit) is a conservative app design choice; ACMA publishes no numeric test and warns inferred consent is less reliable than express consent.

Privacy Act: the small-business exemption is assumed to apply (turnover <= $3M); tranche 2 reforms recommend removing it but no enactment was found. If the business is ever an APP entity, APP 8 (cross-border disclosure to US-hosted providers) and APP 7 (direct marketing) would also apply.
