sources.date_note: Search summary only. It found no video input support. It also quoted a 5 MB per-image limit, which conflicts with the full Vision page (10 MB on the Claude API). The search index is probably stale.

findings.claim: Supported image formats are JPEG, PNG, GIF and WebP. For an animated GIF, only the first frame is used.
findings.evidence: Vision page: "Claude supports JPEG, PNG, GIF, and WebP images (`image/jpeg`, `image/png`, `image/gif`, `image/webp`). Animations are unsupported, and only the first frame is used." The Messages API reference gives the base64 media_type enum as "image/jpeg" or "image/png" or "image/gif" or "image/webp".

findings.claim: The maximum size per image is 10 MB base64-encoded on the first-party Claude API, not 5 MB. 5 MB still applies on Amazon Bedrock.
findings.evidence: "The maximum size per image is: 10 MB (base64-encoded) on the Claude API and Claude Models on Google Cloud (Google managed). 5 MB (base64-encoded) on Amazon Bedrock. 10 MB on claude.ai." The platform metadata for Bedrock says: "Only base64 image sources; per-image limit 5 MB (base64-encoded) and a lower total request size."

findings.claim: The hard pixel limit is 8000x8000 px. A request with more than 20 images gets a stricter per-image limit; keeping every image at or below 3,000 px on each side, or sending at most 20 images, avoids it.
findings.evidence: "The maximum dimensions for each image are 8000x8000 px. If a single API request contains more than 20 images, a stricter per-image dimension limit applies to every image in that request ... To stay under the limit on all platforms, either resize each image so that neither dimension exceeds 3,000 px, or keep the request to 20 or fewer image and document blocks."

findings.claim: The API accepts up to 600 images per request on 1M-context models, which includes Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5. The cap is 100 on 200k-context models. The whole request is limited to 128 MB.
findings.evidence: "100 for each request on the API, for models with a 200k-token context window; 600 for each request on the API, for all other models" and "The limit is 128 MB on the first-party Claude API". API overview table: "Messages, Token Counting | 128 MB"; exceeding it returns 413 request_too_large. Release note of 13 Mar 2026: "We've raised the media limit from 100 to 600 images or PDF pages for each request when using the 1M token context window."

findings.claim: The token cost formula has changed. Visual tokens are now ceil(w/28) x ceil(h/28), with one token per 28x28 patch. The older width*height/750 rule and the 'about 1.15 MP for about 1,600 tokens' guidance no longer match the docs.
findings.evidence: "Claude processes images in patches instead of pixels. Each patch is a 28×28-pixel block of the image, referred to as a visual token. An image, therefore, costs `⌈width / 28⌉ × ⌈height / 28⌉` visual tokens." Example from the table: "1092x1092 px (1.19 megapixels) | Not resized | 1,521".

findings.claim: There are two resolution tiers. The high-resolution tier ("Claude 4.7 and later models") allows a 2,576 px long edge and 4,784 visual tokens. The standard tier allows 1,568 px and 1,568 tokens. Larger images are downscaled automatically unless you opt into an error.
findings.evidence: Table: "High-resolution | Claude 4.7 and later models | 2,576 px | 4,784" / "Standard | All other models | 1,568 px | 1,568". The page also says "High-resolution support is automatic on the listed models and requires no beta header". Example row: "1920x1080 px ... Standard: 1456x819 px, 1,560 tokens ... High-resolution: Not resized, 2,691 tokens."

findings.claim: Claude pads every image on the bottom and right edges to the next multiple of 28 px. Coordinates must be normalised by the resized dimensions, not the padded ones. Setting `transformations.oversized_image: "error"` turns a silent resize into a 400 error, and installed @anthropic-ai/sdk@1.6.0 has this field in its types.
findings.evidence: "Claude then pads every image, resized or not, up to the next multiple of 28 pixels on the bottom and right edges ... Always normalize or rescale by the resized dimensions, not the padded dimensions". Also: "A request whose marked image (any block that sets \"oversized_image\": \"error\") would be resized is rejected with a 400 invalid_request_error". Local check: node_modules/.pnpm/@anthropic-ai+sdk@1.6.0_zod@4.6.7/.../resources/messages/messages.d.ts:3685 has `oversized_image?: 'downsize' | 'error';`.

findings.claim: Images can be sent three ways: base64 inline, a URL the API fetches, or a Files API file_id. Bedrock and Google-managed Vertex accept only base64.
findings.evidence: "provide images to Claude as `image` content blocks using one of three source types: 1. A base64-encoded image embedded in the request body 2. A URL reference to an image hosted online 3. A `file_id` returned by the Files API (upload once, reference many times)". Also: "On Claude Models on Google Cloud (Google managed) and Amazon Bedrock, only base64-encoded sources are available." Release note of 27 Feb 2025 added URL sources.

findings.claim: The Files API went GA on 19 Aug 2026 and needs no beta header. Operations are free, files are up to 500 MB each, with 1 TB per organisation. However, files are not ZDR-eligible, persist until deleted or expired, and any key in the workspace can read them.
findings.evidence: "The Files API is out of beta and needs no beta header." "Maximum file size: 500 MB for each file; Total storage: 1 TB for each organization". "Files API operations are free ... File content used in Messages requests is priced as input tokens." ZDR: "Not eligible ... Files retained until explicitly deleted or they reach their configured expiration." Warning: "Files are not scoped to an end user, conversation, or session. Any API key with access to a workspace can access any files uploaded to that workspace." The page also gives a limit of about 500 file requests per minute.

findings.claim: The API does not accept video input. Current models take text and images and return text, and the Messages API has no video or audio content block, so frames must be extracted client-side.
findings.evidence: Models overview: "All current models support text and image input, text output". Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 overviews: "Input → output | Text and images → text". The Messages API reference lists user content blocks text, image, document, search_result, thinking, redacted_thinking, tool_use, tool_result, server tool results and container_upload; the fetch summary states "No video or audio content block types appear". A WebSearch summary also found no docs supporting video input.

findings.claim: Structured outputs (`output_config.format` with type json_schema) are GA with no beta header and are available on every model, including claude-opus-5-5 and claude-haiku-5-5. The old `output_format` parameter is deprecated.
findings.evidence: Page metadata: "status: stable". supportedModels includes claude-opus-5-5 and claude-haiku-5-5. Availability: "Structured outputs are available on every model". Request shape: "The request carries the schema in `output_config.format` with `type: \"json_schema\"`." Migration note: "The `output_format` parameter is deprecated. To use it anyway, add the `structured-outputs-2025-11-13` beta header. Without it, the API returns a 400 error." Release notes: beta launched 14 Nov 2025; GA and the move to output_config.format on 29 Jan 2026.

findings.claim: Structured-output schemas have limits that affect the label schema design. Across all strict schemas in a request the caps are 20 strict tools, 24 optional parameters and 16 parameters with union types. minimum/maximum/minLength are unsupported, additionalProperties must be false, and enum casing is not guaranteed. Citations and prefill are incompatible; Batch and streaming work.
findings.evidence: Limits table: "Strict tools per request | 20", "Optional parameters | 24", "Parameters with union types | 16". Unsupported: "numerical constraints (minimum, maximum, multipleOf), string constraints (minLength, maxLength)". "Structured outputs don't guarantee the capitalization of string enum and const values". Incompatible with "Citations" and "Message prefilling"; works with "Batch processing", "Token counting" and "Streaming". The page also notes: "Compiled grammars are cached for 24 hours from last use" and "The cache is invalidated if you change the JSON schema structure".

findings.claim: Claude Opus 5.5 costs US$4 input and US$20 output per MTok. Cache writes are $5 (5-minute) or $8 (1-hour), cache hits are $0.20 (0.05x), and Batch is $2 / $10.
findings.evidence: Pricing row: "Claude Opus 5.5 | $4 / MTok | $5 / MTok | $8 / MTok | $0.20 / MTok | $20 / MTok". Batch row: "Claude Opus 5.5 | $2 / MTok | $10 / MTok". The 22 Sep 2026 release note confirms "$4 / $20 USD per MTok".

findings.claim: Claude Haiku 5.5 has two price levels set by prompt length. Up to 100,000 tokens it costs US$0.10 input and US$0.50 output per MTok (5-minute cache write $0.125, 1-hour $0.20, cache hit $0.01, Batch $0.05 / $0.25). Above 100k it costs $0.50 / $2.50.
findings.evidence: "Claude Haiku 5.5 (for prompts up to 100,000 tokens) | $0.10 / MTok | $0.125 / MTok | $0.20 / MTok | $0.01 / MTok | $0.50 / MTok" and "(for prompts over 100,000 tokens) | $0.50 / MTok | $0.625 / MTok | $1 / MTok | $0.05 / MTok | $2.50 / MTok". On prompt length: "A request's prompt length counts all of its input tokens, including cache reads and cache writes."

findings.claim: US-only inference (`inference_geo: "us"`) costs 1.1x; the default is "global". The pages I read document no Australia-only inference option.
findings.evidence: "For Claude 4.6 and later models, using `inference_geo: \"us\"` applies a 1.1x pricing multiplier. `inference_geo: \"global\"` (default) uses standard pricing."

findings.claim: The Message Batches API saves 50% but is asynchronous. Most batches finish within an hour, the worst case is 24 hours before expiry, results are stored for 29 days, and it is not ZDR-eligible. Vision is supported in batches.
findings.evidence: "most batches completing within 1 hour ... Batches expire if processing does not complete within 24 hours." "Batch results are available for 29 days after creation." Metadata: "zdr: eligibility: not-eligible; note: 29-day retention". Vision appears in the list of supported batch features. Limits: "100,000 Message requests or 256 MB".

findings.claim: Rate limits leave plenty of headroom for one shop. On the Start tier, Haiku 5.5 and Opus 5.5 each allow 4,000 RPM, 2,000,000 ITPM and 400,000 OTPM, and cached reads do not count toward ITPM. New organisations may begin in a lower Evaluation tier. The Start tier has a US$500 monthly spend cap. Ramp limits penalise sudden bursts.
findings.evidence: Start tier rows: "Claude Opus 5.5 | 4,000 | 2,000,000 | 400,000" and "Claude Haiku 5.5 | 4,000 | 2,000,000 | 400,000". "New organizations ... may start in the Evaluation tier, with limits below the standard limits". Spend caps: "Start | $500 USD". Ramp limits: "Start scheduled or bulk jobs at a low rate and spread requests evenly".

findings.claim: Haiku 5.5 runs adaptive thinking by default with default effort `medium`. Thinking tokens are billed as output, so effort is the cost lever for labelling. Neither model accepts temperature, top_p or top_k.
findings.evidence: Haiku 5.5 overview: "Adaptive thinking is on by default. Control thinking depth with the effort parameter." and "Omit `temperature`, `top_p`, and `top_k`." Default effort `medium`. Opus 5.5: "Adaptive thinking is always on and can't be turned off." Default effort `medium`. The minimum cacheable prompt is 512 tokens on both.

findings.claim: Usage limits relevant to barbershop footage: Claude will not identify people, and is less reliable on frames under 200 px, rotated frames, exact counts and spatial precision.
findings.evidence: "People identification: Claude cannot be used to name people in images and refuses to do so". "Accuracy: Claude might hallucinate or make mistakes when interpreting low-quality, rotated, or very small images under 200 pixels." "Spatial reasoning: Claude's coordinate and localization outputs are approximate." Tip: "Claude works best when images come before text."

findings.claim: Worked token counts for Studio Assistant frame sizes, using the official formula and reference resize implementation in a local Python check. 432x768 (9:16) costs 448 tokens; 768x432 costs 448; 576x768 (4:3) costs 588; 720x1280 costs 1,196. A 1080x1920 frame is resized to 819x1456 (1,560 tokens) on the standard tier and stays full size (2,691 tokens) on the high-res tier.
findings.evidence: Computed with ⌈w/28⌉×⌈h/28⌉. The 1920x1080 results match the Vision table exactly ("1456x819 px | 1,560" and "Not resized | 2,691"). The Opus 5.5 cost example also matches: "At Claude Opus 5.5's $4 USD per million (high-resolution tier), the same image [1000×1000] costs about $5.18 USD per thousand".

implementation_decision:
AnthropicVisionLabeler (packages/ai), run inside the pg-boss ingest job in apps/worker:

1. Model and settings: keep AI_VISION_MODEL=claude-haiku-5-5. Send output_config.effort="low". Do not send thinking, temperature, top_p, top_k or forced tool_choice. Use non-streaming client.messages.parse with max_tokens of about 4000. Offer claude-opus-5-5 only as an owner-selectable "careful" mode.

2. Frame sampling budget: one frame at each detected shot's midpoint. Add a second frame for shots longer than 5 s, plus the first and last usable frame of the clip for before/after candidates. Pick by quality score and keep at most 12 frames per clip by default. Lower the AI_VISION_MAX_FRAMES_PER_CLIP ceiling from 40 to 20 so a request never exceeds 20 images; above 20 the stricter many-image limit applies and the 10-image default already covers most barber clips.

3. Frame format: extract with ffmpeg after rotation correction and HDR-to-BT.709 tone mapping. Scale the long edge to 768 px, keeping the aspect ratio and even dimensions: 432x768 for 9:16 portrait and 768x432 for landscape, each 448 visual tokens; 4:3 gives 576x768 at 588 tokens. Save as JPEG at about q:v 3. These sizes fit inside both resolution tiers' limits, so neither tier resizes them and the focus {x,y} pixel coordinates map 1:1 onto the frame we sent. Set transformations: { oversized_image: "error" } on every image block to catch drift. Normalise focus by the sent dimensions (432x768), not the padded ones (448x784), and clamp to range. Skip frames under 200 px.

4. Transport: send base64 image blocks in the request body, images first, each followed by a short text label ("Frame 3 · shotId=… · t=4.2 s"), then the instruction text. Do not use the Files API: it is not ZDR-eligible, files persist until deleted, and they are readable workspace-wide. Do not use URL sources: Anthropic would need a fetchable link to private media, which breaks the "media is private" rule. A 12-frame payload is well under the 10 MB per-image and 128 MB per-request limits.

5. Structured outputs: use output_config.format via zodOutputFormat(ShotLabelsSchema) and read response.parsed_output.
   - Mark every property required. Use enums for label and framing. Make focus a single nullable object (one union-type parameter).
   - Validate the 0-1 confidence range and that each shotId is one we sent, in Zod after parsing; the API rejects minimum/maximum.
   - Compare enum values case-insensitively.
   - Keep the schema byte-identical across requests (no per-clip enums) so the compiled grammar is reused for 24 hours.
   - On stop_reason "refusal" or "max_tokens", or on parse failure: retry once, then fall back to HeuristicLabeler's "unknown" labels and mark the clip "needs review". Never invent labels.
   - The prompt must not ask Claude to identify people.

6. Batching: one synchronous Messages request per clip, which matches the per-clip labelShots(frames, context) interface. Run at most 3 clips concurrently per project and spread requests out to avoid ramp limits. Pass the job's AbortSignal to the SDK. Make the job idempotent by storing labels keyed by (assetId, shotId, frame hash).
   - Mark the stable system prompt with cache_control ephemeral (only worth it if it is over 512 tokens).
   - Do not use the Message Batches API for interactive ingest: it can take up to 24 h, keeps data for 29 days, is not ZDR-eligible, and saves under 1 US cent per project. Revisit it only for overnight bulk re-labelling of archives.

7. Cost per project (6 clips × 12 frames, Haiku 5.5, prompts under 100k tokens): 72 × 448 = 32,256 visual tokens. With about 2.1k tokens per request for system prompt, structured-output overhead and context, input is about 7.5k tokens per clip, roughly 45k per project, which is about US$0.0045. Output including adaptive thinking at low effort, assumed 1.5k-3k per clip, adds US$0.0045-0.009. Total is about US$0.01-0.014 per project; at the 20-frame ceiling about US$0.02. The same workload on Opus 5.5 is about US$0.36-0.54, roughly 40 times more. Record the real cost from response.usage in AiUsage.estimatedCostUsdCents and show it in USD; the owner's AUD charge depends on their card's FX rate.
account_requirements: A Claude Console account at platform.claude.com with an organisation. The API overview lists as prerequisites "A Claude Console account" and "An API key from the Console".

An API key, kept server-side only and encrypted at rest as CLAUDE.md requires. Prefer a dedicated workspace with a workspace-scoped key so Studio Assistant traffic, spend and any uploaded data are isolated. If the key is not workspace-scoped, send the anthropic-workspace-id header.

Billing and credits set up in the Console. The org starts in the Evaluation or Start tier; Start has a US$500/month spend cap. Set a lower monthly spend limit (for example US$10-20) under Settings > Spend limits as a guard. Charges are in USD.

No app review, partner approval or beta access is needed. Vision, structured outputs and the Files API are GA with no beta header, and claude-haiku-5-5 and claude-opus-5-5 are self-serve on the Claude API.
Confirm on the supported-regions page that Australia is supported. I did not fetch that page.
Follow the Anthropic Usage Policy: don't ask Claude to identify or name the people in frames (it refuses). Labels must describe the shot, not who is in it.

Data handling choice: use the Messages API with base64 frames. Avoid the Files API and Message Batches, which store data (until deletion, or for 29 days) and are not ZDR-eligible. ZDR itself is an arrangement with Anthropic that this app does not need. Default inference geography is "global" ("us" costs 1.1x), and no Australian residency option is documented. The owner should tell filmed clients that frames are processed by an overseas AI provider; that is the owner's privacy obligation, not something Anthropic's docs cover.
Set AI_PROVIDER=anthropic and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the worker .env. Until both are set, the UI must show an honest "needs setup" state and use HeuristicLabeler.
uncertainties: None of the docs pages show a last-updated date. The visible release notes do not date three changes: the per-image limit moving from 5 MB to 10 MB, the token formula moving from (w*h)/750 to ⌈w/28⌉×⌈h/28⌉, and the transformations.oversized_image field. A WebSearch summary still quoted 5 MB, probably from a stale index. I'm treating the full Vision page (10 MB) as current; the 768 px JPEG frames are far below either figure.

The Vision page assigns the high-resolution tier to "Claude 4.7 and later models" without naming Claude Haiku 5.5. Haiku 5.5 is presumably high-res, but this doesn't matter at 768 px, which fits both tiers without resizing.

The cost estimate assumes about 1.5k-3k output tokens per clip, including adaptive thinking at effort "low", and about 1.5-1.8k tokens of system prompt plus the system prompt that structured outputs injects. Neither figure is documented; measure from response.usage on real footage.
I didn't check, in this session, the per-model rules for turning thinking off on Haiku 5.5 or the exact size of the structured-outputs injected system prompt.
Label quality (before/after/reaction/close-up) of Haiku 5.5 versus Opus 5.5 on barbershop footage is unmeasured. Run a small eval on the owner's own clips before deciding Haiku is good enough.

I didn't fetch Anthropic's API data-retention period for standard Messages requests (the api-and-data-retention page) or the supported-regions page. Australia availability and retention period are therefore unverified here.
The rate-limits page no longer shows credit-purchase thresholds for moving between tiers. Only spend caps (Start US$500, Build US$1,000, Scale US$200,000) and the Evaluation tier note are documented.

The summary of the Messages API reference covered only the first 100k of 143k characters. The content-block list it gave has no video or audio type, and the model pages say "Text and images → text". The no-video conclusion rests on those two sources.

findings.claim: (a) The private-account, SELF_ONLY and 5-users-per-24h rules for unaudited clients are written inside TikTok's Direct Post guidelines, not in any Upload/inbox document.
findings.evidence: In the indexed Content Sharing Guidelines, 'If your API client has not been audited, the following restrictions will apply' introduces a bulleted list, not a heading. The nearest heading above it is the top-level 'Direct Post API - Developer Guidelines' section, which also contains 'Intended Use', 'Required UX Implementation in Your App' and 'Technical Considerations'. The bullets read: 'Unaudited API Clients can allow up to 5 users to post in a 24 hour window. All user accounts using the API client to post must be set to private at the time of posting.' and 'Unaudited API Clients can only post contents in SELF_ONLY viewership.'

findings.claim: (a) The error codes that enforce the unaudited rules are documented only for the Direct Post init endpoint. The inbox init endpoint's error list contains no unaudited or active-user-cap code.
findings.evidence: Direct Post reference: '403 unaudited_client_can_only_post_to_private_accounts' ('unaudited clients can only post to a private account'), and 'The publish attempt will be blocked when calling /publish/video/init/'. It also lists reached_active_user_cap. The Upload reference for POST /v2/post/publish/inbox/video/init/ (scope video.upload) lists only 400 invalid_param, 403 spam_risk_too_many_pending_share, 403 spam_risk_user_banned_from_posting, 403 url_ownership_unverified, 401 access_token_invalid, 401 scope_not_authorized, 429 rate_limit_exceeded and 5xx.

findings.claim: (a) In Upload mode the API cannot set any privacy level, so 'SELF_ONLY' cannot be requested or forced through the inbox init call. The creator chooses visibility in TikTok's editor.
findings.evidence: Upload reference: the request body's required object is source_info, with source FILE_UPLOAD or PULL_FROM_URL and the fields video_size, chunk_size, total_chunk_count or video_url. There is no post_info or privacy_level field. The Photo reference says privacy_level 'is required for DIRECT POST' and must match creator_info options. MEDIA_UPLOAD is described as letting users 'complete the post using TikTok's editing flow'.

findings.claim: (a) TikTok's general wording does not exempt drafts, though. One broadly worded FAQ / Get Started sentence could be read as covering any content from an unaudited client. The official docs neither confirm nor deny that inbox drafts are exempt.
findings.evidence: App Review FAQ and Get Started - Direct Post: 'All content posted by unaudited clients will be restricted to private viewing mode. Once you have successfully tested your integration, to lift the restrictions on content visibility, your API client must undergo an audit to verify compliance with our Terms of Service.' The search tool's own summary: 'The excerpt I retrieved doesn't state the SELF_ONLY or private-account restriction for that flow... I didn't find an explicit statement either way.'

findings.claim: (a) An Upload-specific cap is documented and applies whatever the audit status: at most 5 pending (unfinished) inbox drafts per user in any 24 hours, and 6 init requests per minute per access token. For one owner account the 5-users cap would not matter anyway.
findings.evidence: Upload reference: 403 spam_risk_too_many_pending_share fires when 'the daily upload cap for the API has been reached for the current user', with 'at most 5 pending shares within any 24-hour period'. Also: 'Each user access_token is limited to 6 requests per minute.'

findings.claim: (a) No public source reports a live test in which an unaudited client sent an inbox draft to a public account and the draft was then published publicly. Every community claim that drafts are exempt is untested or rests only on reading the docs.
findings.evidence: xPST PR #266 (26 Sep 2026) says 'inbox-draft is exempt from the privacy restriction', but its follow-up says 'Draft mode (implemented; not live-verified)'. framechester PR #54 (1 Nov 2026): 'A doc do Upload não traz restrição para app não auditado nem para conta privada' (the Upload docs list no restriction for unaudited apps or private accounts), yet 'Envio real ao TikTok: não testado aqui' (real send to TikTok not tested here). faceless PR #22 (22 Oct 2026): 'TikTok's API was tested with mocked answers only.' Crove issue #903 (21 Oct 2026): 'Check TikTok's docs on whether inbox upload has its own audit limits before building.' cogsend PR #1 did test live, but only Direct Post: 'TikTok refuses posts to public accounts until the app is audited.'

findings.claim: (b) Officially, an inbox draft is finished by the creator in TikTok's own editing and creation flow. TikTok counts it as published only after the creator posts it there, and one upload can become several posts.
findings.evidence: Get Started - Upload: the creator 'will receive a notification in their TikTok inbox informing them that their uploaded content is ready for further editing and can be posted through TikTok's creation flow'. Apps 'should inform users that they must click on inbox notifications to continue the editing flow in TikTok and complete the post.' Get Post Status: SEND_TO_USER_INBOX 'Indicates that a notification has been sent to the creator's inbox to complete the draft post using TikTok's editing flow'. PUBLISH_COMPLETE (upload) means 'the user has clicked on the inbox notification and has successfully posted the media using TikTok editing flow', and 'It's possible for the user to make multiple posts from the content associated with one publish_id.'

findings.claim: (b) A TikTok Business Account only gets Commercial Music Library sounds when it taps Add Sound in the app, so in-app editing is where a Commercial Sound would be added. No TikTok doc says outright that Add Sound or public visibility is available on drafts from an unaudited client.
findings.evidence: TikTok Business Help Center (search summary): a Business Account is shown only Commercial Music Library sounds when tapping Add Sound on a new video, while personal accounts see the full library. The Content Posting API docs describe the 'editing flow' but do not list sound selection or say whether an unaudited client's draft can be posted to 'Everyone'. Crove #903 says creators 'add sound and publish inside TikTok', but that is a description of intended behaviour, not a test.

findings.claim: (b) Video inbox uploads probably cannot pre-fill the caption, so the owner would still have to paste it in the TikTok app.
findings.evidence: The Upload init body has no post_info (see above). A third-party report says the 'TikTok Inbox flow ignores post_info — caption empty on draft; Direct Post + video.publish scope is the only fix'. Title and description pre-fill is documented only for photo MEDIA_UPLOAD via /v2/post/publish/content/init/ ('it will be reflected in the editing flow once user clicks on the inbox notification').

findings.claim: (c) The 'utility tool' clause belongs to the Direct Post API developer guidelines that govern the audit. App review, which grants video.upload, has its own and equally decisive bar against private or personal-use apps.
findings.evidence: The Content Sharing Guidelines' 'Intended Use' section sits under 'Direct Post API - Developer Guidelines'. It says clients 'should be intended for a wide audience, not limited to internal groups/private use', and lists as not acceptable: 'A utility tool to help upload contents to the account(s) you or your team manages.' Separately, the App Review Guidelines (app details criteria) say: 'The intended purpose of your app must meet our developer guidelines. Apps must not be for private or personal use. Apps that are still in development or testing will not be approved.' The App Review FAQ adds: 'Beta or development versions, incomplete apps, and test versions are not encouraged and will not be approved for integration with TikTok in most cases.'

findings.claim: (c) video.upload needs an approved app plus the user's own grant. Without the scope, inbox init fails. Review needs a demo video covering every requested scope.
findings.evidence: Get Started - Upload: 'Your app must be approved for the video.upload scope. The target TikTok user must have authorized your app for the video.upload scope.' Upload reference: '401 scope_not_authorized - The access_token does not bear user's grant on video.upload scope.' App Review FAQ: 'All selected products and scopes must be clearly demonstrated in the video.'

findings.claim: A sandbox can test integrations without app review on up to 10 target accounts you own. TikTok's docs exclude public-video posting from the sandbox and do not say whether video.upload inbox drafts work there.
findings.evidence: Add a Sandbox / Introducing Sandbox: 'Sandbox mode is a restricted environment that allows you to try out integrations without having to submit your app for review.' You can create up to 5 sandboxes and share one with up to 10 target users. 'To add a TikTok account that you own as a target user, you must provide its login credentials.' Also: 'Sandbox mode does not offer access to Content Posting API for public videos or Data Portability API.'

findings.claim: Nothing found suggests TikTok changed the Upload/inbox rules in 2025-2026. The guideline pages show August 2026 updates, but no Upload-specific change was found.
findings.evidence: The search found no 2025-2026 Content Posting API changelog entry (latest posting entry 2023; the newest 2026 entry, 21 May, covers Research Tools). Developer Guidelines show 'Last updated August 4, 2026'. cogsend PR #1 says the Content Sharing and App Review Guidelines were 'both updated Aug 4, 2026'. The Photo reference was reportedly updated 27 Oct 2026.

findings.claim: An already audited third-party client (IFTTT) offers an 'Upload video draft' action that sends a video to the creator's TikTok inbox. This is a working inbox-draft route that avoids Studio Assistant's own app review.
findings.evidence: IFTTT TikTok action 'Upload video draft' (search summary): uploads a video to TikTok, the user 'gets a notification in the TikTok app's Inbox', then opens it and chooses to save it as a draft or publish. The 'Video URL' field must link directly to a video file, maximum 4GB. The required plan tier was not stated.

account_requirements: Direct TikTok route (not recommended): a TikTok for Developers account and a registered app with Login Kit and Content Posting API, with the video.upload scope approved in app review. Review requires a demo video that shows every requested scope end to end, a public website with Privacy Policy and ToS, and URL-prefix verification for PULL_FROM_URL. It must also clear the App Review Guidelines bar 'Apps must not be for private or personal use', which a single-business own-account tool is likely to fail.

The owner must personally authorise the app for video.upload through TikTok OAuth (no grant means 401 scope_not_authorized), finish each draft from the TikTok inbox notification, and keep no more than 5 unfinished API drafts in any 24 h.
Commercial Sounds: the owner's TikTok profile must be a Business Account, so that Add Sound shows only the Commercial Music Library.

Sandbox spike (optional): create a sandbox in the developer portal and add the owner's TikTok account as a target user, which means entering its login credentials and agreeing to the Developer Terms. Public-video posting is not available in the sandbox, and video.upload availability there is unconfirmed.

Research environment: allow developers.tiktok.com (and ideally ads.tiktok.com and support.tiktok.com) in this session's network settings, so the official pages can be read in full instead of through search summaries.

Already-audited provider route (if chosen): an account with the provider (Zernio, Buffer or IFTTT; IFTTT's required plan tier is unverified) connected to the owner's TikTok account. The provider needs a direct, time-limited video file URL from Studio Assistant's private media store, never a public permanent link.
uncertainties: The official TikTok pages could not be read in full: developers.tiktok.com returned ENOTFOUND in this sandbox. Every official quote here comes from search-engine snapshots about 100 days old, and the pages may have changed since.

Unknown: whether TikTok enforces the private-account, SELF_ONLY or 5-users rule on inbox drafts in practice. For example, it could force 'Only me' in the editor, or refuse init for an unaudited client targeting a public account. No official statement exists either way, and no public live test was found.

The App Review FAQ sentence 'All content posted by unaudited clients will be restricted to private viewing mode' is not scoped to Direct Post. It could be read as covering drafts the creator later posts from an unaudited client's upload.
Unconfirmed for drafts from an unaudited client: whether TikTok's editing flow offers Add Sound / Commercial Sounds and the 'Everyone' visibility option.
Unknown whether sandbox mode grants video.upload (inbox drafts) at all. The docs only say the sandbox does not offer the Content Posting API 'for public videos'.
Caption pre-fill for video inbox uploads rests on the absence of post_info in the Upload reference plus one third-party report. TikTok docs do not say so explicitly.

Whether TikTok reviewers would grant video.upload to a narrowly scoped own-business app despite the 'private or personal use' bar is unknown. Approval is discretionary and no rejection data specific to video.upload was found.
IFTTT's 'Upload video draft' plan tier, file limits beyond 4GB, and how it handles expiring signed URLs were not verified. The same applies to Zernio's and Buffer's current draft behaviour.

findings.claim: Bottom line: the official access rules allow it, but no one has shown it working. Meta's App Review table exempts Standard Access from App Review for a business you own or manage, under Facebook Login as well as Instagram Login. Unified Login runs on Facebook Login for Business, so the Facebook Login row is the one that applies, not only the 'No login or Instagram Login' row. I found no public report of an actual Reel or image publish from a new Unified-login app in Development mode.
findings.evidence: App Review for Instagram API (search summaries): for an app built for a business the developer owns or manages, the table lists 'No login or Facebook Login' at Standard Access with App Review 'not required', next to 'No login or Instagram Login'. The Tech Provider scenario (serving multiple businesses) needs Advanced Access with App Review under either login type ('Instagram Login | Advanced Access | Required'). Meta's own pages, as summarised, do not name a separate 'Unified Login' row. Community implementations describe Unified login as 'Facebook Login for Business with a config_id' (Postiz #2350, owenpkent, Oct 29, 2026).

findings.claim: Officially, Standard Access permissions can be granted to anyone with a role on the app, and Business Verification is tied only to Advanced Access. Nothing official says business_management behaves differently for role holders.
findings.evidence: Access Levels (search summary): 'Permissions with Standard Access can only be requested from app users who have a role on the requesting app.' Advanced Access 'requires Business Verification'. Apps requesting Advanced Access 'may have to be connected to a verified business' (Feb 1, 2023 rule). Instagram Platform overview: Business Verification is needed 'if your app requires Advanced Access', i.e. when 'the app will be used by people who have no role on the app or on a business that has claimed it'.

findings.claim: (a) Officially, Advanced Access to public_profile is needed only so that people WITHOUT an app role can log in once a Facebook Login for Business app goes live. That contradicts the idea that an app admin needs it to keep business_management.
findings.evidence: Facebook Login for Business (search summary): 'advanced access to the public_profile permission is needed before a Facebook Login for Business app goes live', so that users without an app role (external users) can authorize. Also: 'To serve businesses that you do not own or manage, your app must be approved for Advanced Access via Meta's App Review.' business_management is listed as supported for both user and system-user access tokens.

findings.claim: (a) The claim that business_management is silently dropped under Standard Access rests on one community comment. The same thread says the Unified login permission editor does not offer business_management at all, and that it had to be added through the Facebook Login for Business product's configuration.
findings.evidence: OpenReply #104, kleberncto, Nov 1, 2026 (tested 2026-10-31 on v26.0): 'The token only kept `business_management` on an app with Advanced Access to `public_profile`.' On an app where public_profile was Standard, the consent screen listed the permission but the token dropped it. Before the fix, '`/me/assigned_instagram_accounts` returned `{"data": []}`' and calls 'failed with `100/33`'; after adding business_management it 'returned the account'. The search summary of the same thread says the permission 'wasn't offered in the Unified login permission editor' and was added under the Facebook Login for Business product configuration. OpenPost/Postiz reports also say the Unified login editor 'doesn't offer business_management'. No official Meta statement explains the drop.

findings.claim: (a) Account discovery does not need business_management if the app knows the IG account ID. In the single-business case (app and Instagram account in the same business portfolio), /me/assigned_instagram_accounts is reported empty anyway, yet the system-user token can still read the account.
findings.evidence: Postiz PR #2404, SiyahKale0, Nov 10, 2026: 'If the Meta app and the Instagram account sit in the same business portfolio (pretty common when self-hosting), the token can read and publish to the account, but `/me/assigned_instagram_accounts` is empty.' The code then probes ids from INSTAGRAM_FALLBACK_ACCOUNT_IDS with GET /{id}?fields=id,username. Live run: 'I ran it against a Meta app created on 2026-11-10 with a Creator account. The dialog, token exchange, account selection and channel creation all worked'; '`content_publishing_limit` and media reads succeed with the stored token.' Login requires debug_token scopes instagram_basic and instagram_content_publish. A same-day app cannot have been through App Review, so this was effectively Standard Access. However, 'Publishing, comments and analytics aren't touched', so the publish itself was not shown.

findings.claim: Several other implementers fall back to debug_token granular_scopes.target_ids when the assigned-accounts list is empty. None has verified this against Meta.
findings.evidence: genfeed PR #9676 (Nov 8, 2026) marks the idea that target_ids holds IG account ids on a Unified Login token as 'Unverified against Meta' and says 'Meta's pages I could read do not document the listing edge for these tokens.' Puff2door PR #60 (Nov 8, 2026): 'Meta Unified Login approved @hdsmokeshop.altamonte but the assigned/portfolio edges returned nothing, so connect failed'; the fix 'reads the Instagram target IDs from debug_token granular scopes'. openreply fork PR #8 (Nov 9, 2026): 'A live retry got empty success from all three discovery sources' 'with no Meta errors'.

findings.claim: (b) The official requirements for a System-user access token configuration are a business portfolio you fully control and login through a business portfolio. For testing, the tester needs a role on the app and full control of the client business. Live mode, Business Verification and Tech Provider status do not appear among them. Tech Provider is a scenario label in the App Review table, and the 'Tech Provider + BISU + Embedded Signup' wording comes from WhatsApp docs.
findings.evidence: Facebook Login for Business (search summaries): 'If you select System-user access token, your app receives a business integration system user access token and your app users are required to log in using a business portfolio. This is only required if this configuration needs continuous access to business assets, such as Facebook Pages, ad accounts or Instagram accounts.' 'Your app must be associated with a business portfolio, which you have full control.' For testing, 'the tester must have a role on the app and full control of the client business.' 'Your app can only request logins from web surfaces.' BISU tokens 'default to never expire'. WhatsApp Access Tokens guide: 'If you are a Tech Provider, use a Business Integration System User access token. To generate a Business Integration System User access token, you must implement Embedded Signup (configured with Facebook Login for Businesses)'.

findings.claim: (b) Community runs show SUAT configurations issuing SYSTEM_USER tokens with instagram_content_publish on unpublished (Development mode) apps and on a same-day new app, with no reported verification or review step.
findings.evidence: Postiz #2350, sipaan, Oct 30, 2026: describes the app as 'unpublished / development mode', the setup as 'System-user access token (SUAT)' with expiration Never, and says 'Business portfolio selection is mandatory'. OpenReply #104, Fabre-Play, Oct 30, 2026: 'The exchange succeeds and produces a valid `SYSTEM_USER` token associated with the correct app'; the token includes instagram_content_publish. Postiz PR #2404: 'The default Unified Login configuration issues tokens that never expire (`expires_at: 0`)'.

findings.claim: (c) A user-access-token configuration is reportedly NOT a working alternative under Unified login, because it offers no Instagram permissions. The classic Facebook dialog with an explicit scope list is rejected for new apps.
findings.evidence: Postiz #2350, owenpkent, Oct 29, 2026: a User access token configuration 'offers no permissions to select' ('No matching results'); 'The Instagram permissions are only offered on System-user access token configurations'; scope error 'Invalid Scopes: instagram_basic, pages_show_list, pages_read_engagement, business_management'. Postiz PR #2404: 'Instagram (Facebook Business) fails with `Invalid Scopes`, because these apps only accept a `config_id`.' Official FLfB docs say business_management works with both token types, but say nothing about Instagram permissions in user-token configurations under Unified login.

findings.claim: (d) Meta has NOT confirmed in its documentation, changelog or blog that Instagram Login is gone for new apps. The evidence is Meta's own App Dashboard text plus an OAuth error, both reported independently by several developers between Oct 29 and Nov 10, 2026. Meta's docs only call Unified Login 'recommended for new integrations' and still document Instagram Login.
findings.evidence: Dashboard text quoted by owenpkent (Oct 29), sipaan (Oct 30), OpenPost #495 (Oct 31) and SiyahKale0 (Nov 10, 2026): 'API setup with Instagram login is not available for newer apps. Your app uses API setup with Unified login instead.' Postiz PR #2404: 'Instagram (Standalone) fails with `Invalid Request: Request parameters are invalid: Invalid platform app`' and 'There's no separate Instagram app ID anymore.' Official Instagram Platform page: 'The Instagram API with Unified Login is the recommended setup for new integrations.' Changelog search: latest entries June-July 2026, Instagram Login still documented, no deprecation entry found.

findings.claim: A possible single-business alternative to the OAuth dialog: a system user token generated in the owner's own Business Settings. Officially this needs only Standard Access and the app and system user in the same business. Whether Instagram publish permissions are offered there for a new Unified-login app is unverified.
findings.evidence: System Users docs (search summary): 'To create a system user access token, this app must have Standard Access. You can also contact your Facebook representative to be added to a list of businesses allowed to create the token.' 'A system user can only be granted a role on an app if both the system user and the app belong to the same business.' 'A system user or an admin system user must install the app that will be used for generating an access token.'

implementation_decision:
Keep direct Reels publishing as an option, but do not make it the default. Ship 'export and post manually' (as for TikTok) as the guaranteed path. Turn direct publish on only after the owner's own app passes a live smoke test.

1. Auth: build one Instagram adapter, Unified Login, as a Facebook Login for Business 'System-user access token' configuration.
   - Dialog: facebook.com/{v}/dialog/oauth with client_id, config_id, response_type=code and override_default_response_type=true, no scope.
   - Exchange the code server-side on graph.facebook.com. Encrypt and store the token.
   - Run debug_token and require type SYSTEM_USER plus the scopes instagram_basic and instagram_content_publish. If they are missing, show 'needs setup'.
   - Do NOT build the Instagram Login fallback or a user-access-token configuration now. New apps reportedly cannot use Instagram Login ('Invalid platform app'), and user-token configurations reportedly offer no Instagram permissions. Keep the adapter interface so Instagram Login can be added later if the owner turns out to have a pre-Oct-2026 app.

2. Account discovery must not depend on business_management:
   - (i) Call GET /me/assigned_instagram_accounts.
   - (ii) If it is empty, read the instagram_basic / instagram_content_publish target_ids from debug_token granular_scopes.
   - (iii) If that is also empty, let the owner type in their IG user ID and probe GET /{id}?fields=id,username.
   - Store the resolved ID. If all three fail, show the honest 'needs setup' state, with the hint to add business_management to the configuration and reconnect.

3. Stay in Development mode with Standard Access. Only the owner (app Admin, full control of the business portfolio) connects. No public connect flow, no App Review, no Business Verification. Any staff member who connects also needs an app role and full control of the portfolio.

4. Gate direct publish behind a recorded smoke test: one REELS container, poll status_code until FINISHED, then media_publish to the owner's account. Until that passes, the UI shows Instagram as 'export and post manually'.

5. If Meta ever returns a permission or review error for role holders, switch the integration to manual-only. Do not request Advanced Access unless the business decides to serve accounts it does not own.
account_requirements: An Instagram professional account (Business or Creator) owned by the studio.
A Meta developer account for the owner, who must be an Admin on the Meta app. Anyone else who connects also needs an app role (Admin/Developer/Tester).

A Meta business portfolio the owner has full control of. The Meta app must be connected to it, and the Instagram account must be added to or claimed by it, with the owner holding full control of the Instagram asset. The Facebook Login for Business docs say the tester must have 'a role on the app and full control of the client business'.
A new Meta app with the 'Manage messaging & content on Instagram' use case (expect 'API setup with Unified login'), with the Facebook Login for Business product added.

One Facebook Login for Business configuration: access token type 'System-user access token', expiry Never (or 60 days plus a reconnect reminder), Instagram account as the business asset, permissions instagram_basic and instagram_content_publish. Optionally add business_management through Facebook Login for Business > Configurations if account discovery comes back empty. Record the config_id.
A valid HTTPS OAuth redirect URI, saved both in the configuration and in Facebook Login for Business > Valid OAuth Redirect URIs. Logins must come from a web surface.
The app stays in Development mode at Standard Access. No App Review, Business Verification, Tech Provider status or Live mode is needed while only role holders connect their own business's account.
Only if the studio later serves accounts it does not own: Advanced Access through App Review, plus Business Verification, plus Advanced Access to public_profile before going live.

No Facebook Page is needed for Unified Login (community reports citing Meta's Unified login docs). If the Instagram account is already linked to a Page, the owner must keep admin-equivalent Page access.
uncertainties: developers.facebook.com could not be reached from this sandbox (ENOTFOUND), so I read none of Meta's own pages in full. The official 'Instagram API with Unified Login' page was not read at all, not even as a search snippet. All official wording above comes from search summaries. findings.claim: In Square Appointments the no-show fee is not only per service. Under 'Hold card in case of no-show' the seller picks a mode: a flat fee per appointment (business-wide), a flat fee per service, or, in some regions, a percentage of each service price. Australia offers both the per-appointment and per-service flat fees.
findings.evidence: Summaries of article 5493: 'You'll have three fee options with no-show protection: to charge a flat fee per appointment, per service, or as a percentage of each service price.' Steps: 'Appointments > Settings > Payments & cancellations… select Hold card in case of no-show > Next… Select Flat fee per service. Choose services > select Done. Add a Fee amount. Select Save.' A summary of the AU page said 'there is a $500 limit if you set your cancellation fee per appointment' and 'at the moment, there isn't a way to charge a percentage-based No-Show Protection fee across all of your services.' The CA blog gives a $650 per-appointment limit instead. I could not read the AU page in full to confirm its exact current menu labels.

findings.claim: In per-service mode, each service is configured separately. A service with no fee entered carries no no-show protection, so a mix of fee-bearing and fee-free services is possible.
findings.evidence: Square help: 'A cancellation fee amount must be entered for each service in your catalog or you won't be able to charge a cancellation fee.' Community: 'you have selected Fee for each service within the Cancellation Fee settings section, and never assigned a cancellation fee to the particular service being booked' (no card is requested in that case). CA blog: per-service fees 'default to 50% of the total service charge for services created in-app, $0 for services created online.'

findings.claim: The API exposes the fee at two levels. A per-variation no_show_fee is returned in raw catalog JSON, but it is undocumented and missing from the SDK types. A business-level cancellation_fee_money is documented.
findings.evidence: A search summary of the docs' 'Search for appointment services' example: one variation's item_variation_data 'includes a no_show_fee object with an amount of 2500 in USD, alongside a price of 8000 and a service duration. The example's Power Clean variation has no no_show_fee field at all.' Docs: 'the non-zero cancellation fee (as expressed by the no_show_fee object) is set in the Square Dashboard. It cannot be set using the Bookings API.' The CatalogItemVariation reference does not list no_show_fee. The square@46.0.0 types confirm this: CatalogItemVariation.d.ts has no noShowFee, and BusinessAppointmentSettings.d.ts has '/** The flat-fee amount charged for a no-show booking. */ cancellationFeeMoney?: Square.Money;'. Response parsing in the SDK uses unrecognizedObjectKeys 'passthrough', which keeps unknown keys under their raw name. So a raw 'no_show_fee' key should survive on itemVariationData, though I did not test this live.

findings.claim: Officially, the booking restriction is worded per service: a service whose no_show_fee is non-zero cannot be booked through the Bookings API. A second docs page words it more broadly, as no booking with a non-zero cancellation fee.
findings.evidence: Create and Manage Bookings: 'You cannot use the Bookings API to book a service that has a non-zero cancellation fee set on its no_show_fee attribute.' Bookings API Concepts: 'You cannot currently use the Bookings API to create a booking with a non-zero cancellation fee. You must use the Square Dashboard to do that.' I found no changelog entry lifting this restriction.

findings.claim: No source says whether a non-zero business-level cancellation_fee_money (the per-appointment flat fee) blocks API creates for every service. No source covers UpdateBooking (reschedule) or CancelBooking on a fee-protected booking either.
findings.evidence: Several extended searches of developer.squareup.com found nothing on this. One summary said: 'Nothing I found says whether a time change on a no-show-protected booking is permitted. The only way to confirm is to test it in the sandbox.' Inference only, unverified: if cancellation_fee_money is the per-appointment flat fee, every booking carries a fee, so the Concepts wording would block every API create.

findings.claim: The error category, code and detail string returned when a write is blocked for this reason are not publicly documented.
findings.evidence: Searches for BAD_REQUEST, INVALID_REQUEST_ERROR and FORBIDDEN together with no-show or cancellation fee found nothing. Summary: 'I found no source that confirms the exact error code returned when a fee-bearing service is booked via API.' The only nearby forum error (thread 1746) is a BAD_REQUEST for a team member who is not bookable, which is a different cause. The 403 for missing Appointments Plus or Premium is a separate failure (see the earlier decision, support_seller_level_writes).

findings.claim: Square's 2026 forum answer on the Australian barbershop thread says there is no supported native way to keep no-show protection on API bookings. It suggests excluding fee-bearing variations and building protection yourself with the Cards and Payments APIs.
findings.evidence: Summaries of thread 28018: 'the Bookings API has no supported way to book a service with no-show protection natively. It cannot create bookings for service variations with a non-zero no_show_fee'. It recommends 'configuring the initial Catalog Search using filters that would exclude those options' and says: 'A supported option is to save the customer's card with the Cards API after they agree to your no-show policy. If they don't show up, charge the fee with the Payments API using that card.' Also: 'there is no supported way today to link a Payments API payment to a booking'. Booking changes made through the API still send Square's standard customer notifications, and 'All of this works in Australia.' I could not confirm whether a Square staff member wrote the reply.

findings.claim: A third-party vendor claims seller-level access can book fee-bearing services, with the booking ACCEPTED immediately and the fee enforced afterwards. This contradicts Square's docs and is unverified.
findings.evidence: iBooker: 'Booking a service that carries a cancellation or no-show fee requires seller-level API access, and at that access level Square's API always creates the appointment as Accepted'. It also says 'Your cancellation policy and no-show fee still apply in full'. Another iBooker page says it requests buyer-level scopes, so the vendor's own pages are inconsistent.

findings.claim: No 2025–2026 change to how no-show fees interact with the Bookings API was found. Third-party 2026 sources say no-show protection needs Plus or Premium, but I did not verify this on Square's AU pricing page.
findings.evidence: Search summary: 'I didn't find any announced 2026 change to Square Appointments' no-show, late-cancellation, or prepayment rules.' Third-party AU reviews say no-show protection, custom cancellation policies and the waitlist require Plus or Premium, and list Plus at A$40 and Premium at A$90 per location per month. A community answer says late-cancellation and no-show fees are not configured separately.

implementation_decision:
Replace the assumption 'keep fee-free variations'. Treat no-show protection as a runtime property that Studio Assistant detects and reports honestly.

(1) Detect. On connect and in the nightly reconcile, read BusinessBookingProfile.business_appointment_settings.cancellation_fee_money and each APPOINTMENTS_SERVICE variation's raw `no_show_fee`. The square@46 SDK keeps it as a passthrough snake_case key on itemVariationData. Add it as an optional field in the packages/core Zod schema and never assume it is present. Classify each variation:
- 'Bookable from Studio Assistant': no variation fee and a business flat fee of zero.
- 'Book in Square': variation no_show_fee is non-zero.
- 'Unverified': business-level cancellation_fee_money is non-zero, which most likely means the flat fee per appointment, so every service carries a fee.

(2) Gate Tier 1 per variation, not per business. Create and reschedule are enabled only for bookable variations, and the reschedule check uses the booking's segments. While the status is unverified, disable create and reschedule. Explain it in the UI (Australian English): 'Your no-show fee applies to every appointment, and Square doesn't let other apps book appointments that carry a no-show fee. Book these in Square Appointments.' Link to the Square booking. Leave cancel enabled but send it as a guarded call.

(3) Errors. Square does not document an error code for this case. On any 4xx from CreateBooking, UpdateBooking or CancelBooking, store the category, code, detail and field verbatim, mark that variation as 'Book in Square', and show 'Square declined this change'. Never show a booking as made. A 403 still switches the module to read-only (plan missing). Do not retry 4xx responses; keep idempotency keys.

(4) Plan advice in Settings.
- Owner uses a flat fee per appointment: say that Tier 1 writes are expected not to work, so paying for Plus only to get them is not advised. Tier 0 (reads, webhooks, attendance heuristic) works on any plan. If the owner already pays for Plus to get no-show protection, Tier 1 costs nothing extra but is limited in the same way.
- Owner switches to a flat fee per service: they can leave chosen variations fee-free (for example 'Phone/walk-in booking'). Staff-made bookings of those variations work through the API but carry no card hold. Online bookings in Square keep full protection.

(5) Do not build the Cards API and Payments API card-on-file workaround now. It needs PAYMENTS_WRITE, card capture through the Web Payments SDK, recorded customer consent to the policy, and manual reconciliation because payments cannot be linked to bookings. Record it as a later option.

(6) Before Tier 1 ships, run a sandbox test (Appointments Plus test subscription) with three set-ups: a per-service fee on one variation and not another; a per-appointment flat fee; and no fee. In each, call seller-level CreateBooking, UpdateBooking (time change) and CancelBooking. Record the exact error responses and update the classifier and copy. Until that test passes, the per-appointment rule stays 'unverified', not 'confirmed'.
account_requirements: Square seller account in Australia with Square Appointments activated. Tier 0 reads and webhooks work on the Free plan.

Square Appointments Plus (about A$40/month per location) or Premium (about A$90/month per location) for seller-level create, update and cancel. Confirm at runtime with RetrieveBusinessBookingProfile.support_seller_level_writes === true. Third-party sources say no-show protection itself also needs Plus or Premium, but this is not verified on Square's AU pricing page.

OAuth scopes: APPOINTMENTS_WRITE and APPOINTMENTS_ALL_WRITE for writes; APPOINTMENTS_BUSINESS_SETTINGS_READ to read cancellation_fee_money; ITEMS_READ to read variation no_show_fee; APPOINTMENTS_READ and APPOINTMENTS_ALL_READ.

Owner checks the no-show set-up under Square Dashboard > Appointments > Settings > Payments & cancellations. If the mode is 'flat fee per appointment', expect app bookings not to work. If the mode is 'flat fee per service', choose which variations stay fee-free (no card hold) so staff can make them from Studio Assistant. Bookings of fee-bearing services stay in Square Appointments or the Square booking site.
Owner understands that a booking made through the API carries no card hold, and Square still sends its standard customer notifications for API changes.

Developer: a Square sandbox test account onboarded to Appointments, with a sandbox Appointments Plus subscription paid with a test card. Run the three fee set-ups described in the decision and record the actual error responses before shipping Tier 1.

Not needed now, only if card-on-file protection is wanted later: PAYMENTS_WRITE, Cards API card capture through the Web Payments SDK with recorded customer consent to the no-show policy, and manual reconciliation because payments cannot be linked to bookings.
Session network: developer.squareup.com and squareup.com must be allowed in this session's network settings so the official pages can be read in full and these findings re-checked.
uncertainties: Exact error response unknown: Square documents no category, code or detail for a write refused because of a no-show fee. It has to be captured in the sandbox.

Unclear whether a non-zero business-level cancellation_fee_money (presumed to be the 'flat fee per appointment' mode) blocks seller-level CreateBooking for every service. The docs word the rule per service (no_show_fee) on one page and per booking ('non-zero cancellation fee') on another. That cancellation_fee_money corresponds to the per-appointment mode is my inference, not documented.
No source covers whether UpdateBooking (reschedule) or CancelBooking fails on a booking whose service carries a fee, or on a booking created in Square with a held card.

The per-variation no_show_fee appears only in a docs example response. It is undocumented in the CatalogItemVariation reference and absent from square@46.0.0 types, so Square could rename or remove it. I did not test live that it survives SDK parsing as a passthrough key.
The third-party iBooker claim that seller-level access can book fee-bearing services contradicts Square's docs and is unverified.

I relied on search summaries only: both developer.squareup.com and squareup.com failed with ENOTFOUND, so no official page was read in full and no last-updated dates were visible. The help-article summaries mixed regional versions (AU, US, GB, IE, CA), so the AU per-appointment cap ($500 reported, versus $650 for CA) and the current AU menu labels need confirming.

The forum thread's authorship is unconfirmed: I could not see whether the reply in thread 28018 came from Square staff. Its age (about 46 days, roughly late September 2026) comes from search summaries.
Unverified on Square's AU pricing page: whether no-show protection requires Plus or Premium in Australia in 2026 (third-party sources say yes).
